<!-- source: python-tour.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/python-tour.md -->

---
title: Python tour (notebook)
audience: users
kind: tutorial
summary: Walk through the bundled Leavenworth fixture end-to-end in a notebook — map, validation report, quality report, simplify-geometry diff, scope visualization. For the browser version, see the Visual tour.
---

# Python tour (notebook)

## What you'll build

You'll work through the bundled Leavenworth, WA network in one notebook session and produce, in order:

1. A folium / matplotlib map of the full network.
2. A validation report rendered as an HTML card.
3. A data-quality report grouped by severity.
4. A simplify-geometry edit, rendered as a before/after diff (then rolled back).
5. A scoped subgraph around a single node, rendered side-by-side with the original.

Total runtime: under two minutes on a laptop. The fixture ships inside the `netstead` wheel (the CSV flavour is about 140 KB).

## Prerequisites

The `[clean]` extra brings in `shapely` + `geopandas` + `pyproj` for the geometry edit; `[graph]` brings in `scipy` for the scope step and the data-quality rule pack; `[notebook]` is reserved for future widgets — the `_repr_html_` cards used below render without it.

`netstead` 1.0.0b2 is not on PyPI yet, so the beta installs from GitHub (both packages in one command; see [Install and troubleshoot](install.md)):

```bash
pip install \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[clean,graph,notebook] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"
```

For the map steps, either `folium` (interactive Leaflet) or `matplotlib` (static fallback) works — pick one:

```bash
pip install folium       # interactive Leaflet map
pip install matplotlib   # static fallback
```

The steps below show both paths.

## Steps

### 1. Load the fixture

Start by loading the bundled Leavenworth network. `Network.from_source` returns a lazy `Network` — no rows have been read from disk yet; `net.links` is a lazy `Table` (the underlying ibis expression is at `net.links.expr`).
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
print(f"{net.spec_version}: {net.links.count()} links, {net.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

You should see:

```text
0.97: 339 links, 121 nodes
```

In a notebook, evaluating `net` on its own renders an HTML summary card with the spec version, the 9 tables with their row counts, and a preview of the first rows.

![Network summary card](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-network-card.png){ .screenshot }
*Network summary card (net._repr_html_()) — spec 0.97, 9 tables, 339 links / 121 nodes, first-rows preview*

### 2. Render the network as a map

The `link` table is keyed to `geometry` by `geometry_id`; the `geometry.geometry` column carries each link's LineString as WKB bytes in memory (the CSV on disk stores WKT; netstead decodes it on load). Materialize both with `.to_pandas()`, join them, and decode the WKB with shapely before plotting.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
import pandas as pd
from shapely import wkb

links = net.links.to_pandas()
geoms = net.tables["geometry"].to_pandas().set_index("geometry_id")
links = links.join(geoms[["geometry"]], on="geometry_id")
links["shape"] = links["geometry"].map(wkb.loads)
```

For an interactive Leaflet map, use folium. Compute the centroid from the node table, then add one PolyLine per link.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
import folium

# Centroid of the network — average node y/x
nodes = net.nodes.to_pandas()
center = [nodes["y_coord"].mean(), nodes["x_coord"].mean()]

m = folium.Map(location=center, zoom_start=15, tiles="OpenStreetMap")
for shape in links["shape"]:
    coords = [(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords]  # folium wants (lat, lon)
    folium.PolyLine(coords, color="#1f77b4", weight=2, opacity=0.8).add_to(m)
m  # in a notebook, this renders the map inline
```

You should see the downtown Leavenworth grid — a compact, walkable core wrapped around Highway 2 / Front Street, surrounded by a few residential tertiary streets.

![Folium map of the full Leavenworth fixture](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-folium-map.png){ .screenshot }
*Folium map of the full Leavenworth fixture — downtown grid around Highway 2 with residential streets fanning out*

If `folium` isn't available, the static matplotlib fallback gives an equivalent view (without basemap tiles):
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
for shape in links["shape"]:
    xs, ys = shape.xy
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color="#1f77b4", linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.8)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title(f"Leavenworth GMNS fixture — {len(links)} links")
plt.show()
```

Either way: a recognizable Bavarian-themed downtown core in an OSM-derived street network roughly 2 km across.

### 3. Validate and display the report

`net.validate()` runs the four-pass validator (structural / schema / FK / sync-state) and returns a `ValidationReport`. In a notebook, evaluating the report on its own renders a styled HTML card.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
report = net.validate()
report  # in a notebook, the _repr_html_ renders a styled card
```

You should see a card with no ERRORs, no WARNINGs and 16 INFO findings. The INFOs are `structural.missing_optional_resource`, one per optional GMNS table the fixture doesn't include. INFO findings don't count against cleanliness, so `report.is_clean` is `True`.

![Validation report card](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-validation-report.png){ .screenshot }
*Validation report card — 0 ERRORs, 0 WARNINGs, 16 INFO structural.missing_optional_resource across 9 tables*

In a non-notebook context, drop down to the text representation:
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
print(f"{report.spec_version}: {len(report.issues)} issues")
for issue in report.issues[:5]:
    print(f"  {issue.severity.value:9} {issue.code:30} {issue.message[:60]}")
```

### 4. Run quality and display

The data-quality pack flags things the spec is silent on but every real network has — disconnected components, lane-count mismatches, high speeds on residential facilities, near-duplicate nodes. Run it the same way as validation; the result has its own `_repr_html_`.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
from corral.quality import run_quality

qreport = run_quality(net)
qreport  # _repr_html_ renders severity-grouped findings
```

You should see a card of WARNING findings (no ERRORs): 271 links with `facility_type=residential` carry `free_speed=40`, above the default 35 mph threshold of `quality.high_speed_residential` — useful for seeing what a real finding looks like, with its `fix_hint`.

![Quality report card](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-quality-report.png){ .screenshot }
*Quality report card — 271 WARNING quality.high_speed_residential findings (residential links with free_speed=40, default 35 mph threshold)*

To see the top findings in detail, iterate over `qreport.issues`:
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
for issue in qreport.issues[:3]:
    print(f"  {issue.severity.value:9} {issue.code:35} {issue.message}")
```

### 5. Simplify geometry and render before/after

The `simplify_geometry` op in `netstead.clean` removes redundant vertices from link geometries. Leavenworth keeps its shapes in the `geometry` table (keyed by `link.geometry_id`), so the op edits that table directly; no inline `link.geometry` column is needed. Wrap it in a `Session` so the edit can be rolled back atomically.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
from corral.editing import Session
from netstead.clean import simplify_geometry

with Session(net) as s:
    edit = simplify_geometry(net, s, mode="redundant_only", tolerance=0.000001)
    edit  # in a notebook, _repr_html_ shows the diff card (the edit targets the geometry table)
```

You should see an `EditResult` card for the `geometry` table: the op and table, the `+added / -removed / ~changed` row counts, the session id and the timestamp. `mode="redundant_only"` drops vertices that sit on the chord through their neighbours; with `tolerance=0.0` it is loss-free, and the 0.000001-degree (about 10 cm) tolerance here also catches the near-collinear vertices OSM traces leave behind, removing about a third of Leavenworth's 2,132 vertices. `mode="douglas_peucker"` is the lossy alternative with an explicit tolerance.

![EditResult card for the simplify-geometry edit](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-simplify-edit-result.png){ .screenshot }
*EditResult card for the simplify-geometry edit: the op and the `geometry` table, the changed-row count, session id and timestamp.*

To visualize before-and-after on one map, keep the decoded shapes from step 2 as the "before" set, then read the edited `geometry` table as the "after" set:
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
links_before = links[["link_id", "shape"]].copy()
# (run the simplify edit above inside the Session)
geoms_after = net.tables["geometry"].to_pandas().set_index("geometry_id")
links_after = links.copy()
links_after["shape"] = links_after["geometry_id"].map(lambda gid: wkb.loads(geoms_after.loc[gid, "geometry"]))

m = folium.Map(location=center, zoom_start=15, tiles="OpenStreetMap")
for shape in links_before["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#888", weight=4, opacity=0.4).add_to(m)
for shape in links_after["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#d62728", weight=1.5, opacity=0.9).add_to(m)
m
```

Grey underneath = before; red on top = after. The two overlays sit almost exactly on top of each other, because the dropped vertices were within 10 cm of a straight line, so look for the red line cutting the tiny kinks on the curved tertiary links.

To restore the original state, roll the session back:
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
s.rollback()
```

The session's chronological log reverses the edit, so the network returns to step 1: 339 links, with every vertex back in the `geometry` table.

### 6. Build a scope from a single node and render

`from_node` builds a network-distance-bounded subgraph around a seed node. The 200 m buffer below is Dijkstra-bounded along the routable graph — links that are spatially close but only reachable via long detours fall outside.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
from netstead.scope import from_node

scoped = from_node(net, node_id=1, network_buffer="200m").apply()
print(f"scoped: {scoped.links.count()} links, {scoped.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

You should see `scoped: 8 links, 5 nodes`. Every related table (`lane`, `link_tod`, `movement`, signal tables) is pre-filtered by FK chain, so the result is a self-consistent GMNS network you can write back out.

Render the scope side-by-side with the original to see the contrast — full network as grey context, scoped subgraph highlighted.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

```python
scoped_links = scoped.links.to_pandas().join(geoms[["geometry"]], on="geometry_id")
scoped_links["shape"] = scoped_links["geometry"].map(wkb.loads)

m = folium.Map(location=center, zoom_start=15, tiles="OpenStreetMap")
# Full network, faint
for shape in links["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#bbb", weight=1, opacity=0.5).add_to(m)
# Scope, highlighted
for shape in scoped_links["shape"]:
    folium.PolyLine([(y, x) for x, y in shape.coords],
                    color="#2ca02c", weight=3, opacity=0.95).add_to(m)
m
```

You should see a small green subgraph centered on one intersection, with the rest of the network greyed out as context.

![Scoped subgraph](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-scoped-map.png){ .screenshot }
*Scoped subgraph (200 m network buffer around node 1, green) over the full Leavenworth network (grey)*

## Variations you might try

Each accordion below is a one-line tweak that shows off a different facet of the toolkit. Pick whichever matches what you want to learn next.

???+ note "Try a different fixture or your own network"
    The bundled fixture is Leavenworth. Point `Network.from_source` at any GMNS package on disk or in cloud storage to repeat the tour with your own data — every step above is fixture-agnostic.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

    ```python
    net = Network.from_source("./my-network/")
    net = Network.from_source("s3://my-bucket/network.parquet/")
    ```

??? note "Configure a custom quality threshold"
    Override the `quality.high_speed_residential` threshold (default is conservative). Tightening it surfaces more findings on a network with mixed posted speeds.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

    ```python
    from corral.quality import RuleConfig, run_quality

    qreport = run_quality(
        net,
        config={
            "quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(
                thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 30.0}
            )
        },
    )
    ```

## Next steps

* [Cookbook](cookbook/index.md) — task-oriented recipes for any of the workflows above.
* [API reference](reference/api.md) — every symbol you used in this tour.
* [Architecture](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/architecture/) — design rationale for sessions, scopes, and the lazy-by-default engine.
* [Table of tables](reference/table-of-tables.md) — what other GMNS tables you can pull from `net.tables[...]`.


<!-- source: workbench-and-other-tools.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/workbench-and-other-tools.md -->

---
title: The Workbench and other tools
audience: users
kind: concept
summary: How the Netstead Workbench differs from GeoLibre, QGIS, ArcGIS and the GMNS modelling tools, and how to use them together.
---

# The Workbench and other tools

## What it is

The Netstead Workbench is a **network session**, not a GIS. It holds one or more GMNS networks in a live
DuckDB session and gives them a map and linked tables. What it adds that a GIS does not:

* **Spec-aware tables.** Foreign keys from the GMNS spec drive navigation, related-row tints, validation and
  cascading deletes across `link`, `node`, `lane`, `segment` and the rest.
* **Selections that resolve.** A phrase such as "I-90 EB between Exit 85 and Exit 87" becomes a path with
  anchors, candidates, confidence and diagnostics, and can be pinned, saved and exported.
* **Edits with an audit trail.** Every change is a typed action with undo, lineage, "copy as Python" and,
  through plugins, ProjectCard output.
* **Validation on the map.** Issues link to rows and markers; a fix is an edit, not a redraw.

What it deliberately leaves to other tools: cartography beyond color-by, width-by and filter; context layers
such as aerials, land use or census data; printing; 3D; and running a model.

## Why we have it

Transportation networks are relational, and GIS tools see one layer at a time. The Workbench exists so that
the relational work (does this lane belong to that link, does this edit break a movement, which links does
this phrase mean) happens in one place with a map attached, and so that the result can be handed to a GIS
or a model in a format it already reads.

## Mental model

Three roles, one network:

| Role | Tool | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| Network session | Netstead Workbench | tables, selection, validation, edits, history |
| GIS canvas | GeoLibre, QGIS, ArcGIS Pro | symbology, legends, context layers, print, 3D |
| Model engine | AequilibraE, DTALite, Path4GMNS, commercial packages | assignment, simulation, skims |

The hand-off between roles is a file. A network saved from the Workbench as Parquet is a directory of one
GeoParquet file per table, which every GIS canvas and most model engines open directly. Save it from
**Edits → Save a copy** with the Parquet format, or from Python:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
net.write("./leavenworth.parquet")
```

Expected: a `leavenworth.parquet/` directory holding `link.parquet`, `node.parquet`, `geometry.parquet` and the
other tables the network carries. Shapes live wherever the network keeps them: on `link` when it has its own
geometry column, otherwise in `geometry` keyed by `geometry_id`, with nodes as `x_coord` / `y_coord` points.

## How it relates to ...

### GeoLibre

[GeoLibre](https://github.com/opengeos/GeoLibre) is a client-side GIS from the
[opengeos](https://github.com/opengeos) group: MapLibre and deck.gl rendering, DuckDB-WASM for import and SQL,
a large toolbox compiled to WebAssembly, and the same React app shipped as a desktop program, a web app and a
Jupyter widget. Its plugins are JavaScript bundles that add panels, controls and layers; Python drives it as a
widget but cannot extend its UI.

The two are complementary rather than competing. GeoLibre is the better canvas: categorised and graduated
symbology, legends, print layouts, basemaps, time slider, 3D, and any GeoParquet, COG, PMTiles or service layer
dropped beside the network. The Workbench is the better session: it keeps the network's tables, selection and
edit history, which GeoLibre's per-layer feature model has no place for.

Use them together by saving from the Workbench and opening in GeoLibre, on the desktop or from a notebook
with its `add_geoparquet`. A thin GeoLibre plugin that connects to a running `netstead app` and mirrors the
selection both ways is a natural later step; the Workbench's action API is designed to be driven that way.

### QGIS

[QGIS](https://qgis.org) reads GeoParquet natively in recent releases (3.36 and later, where its GDAL build
includes the Arrow driver) and CSV with WKT through its delimited-text layer. It is the usual desktop home
for cartography and for joining a network to parcels, zones or counts. The GMNS community's
[NeXTA4GMNS](https://github.com/asu-trans-ai-lab/NeXTA4GMNS) notes describe viewing and editing GMNS in QGIS.

Edits made in QGIS do not come back with lineage. Make attribute edits in the Workbench and use QGIS for
geometry work and maps.

### ArcGIS Pro

[ArcGIS Pro](https://www.esri.com/en-us/arcgis/products/arcgis-pro/overview) reads GeoParquet from 3.3 on,
and its Network Analyst extension builds routable network datasets from feature classes. The Workbench is
the place to validate and fix a GMNS network before it becomes such a dataset; ArcGIS is the place to publish
it as a feature service or run Network Analyst solvers on it.

### Network Wrangler and ProjectCard

[Network Wrangler](https://github.com/network-wrangler/network_wrangler) manages scenarios as a base network
plus an ordered set of [ProjectCards](https://github.com/network-wrangler/projectcard). Netstead reads and
writes the card format rather than depending on Wrangler's pandas stack: Workbench selections export as card
facility objects, the fix workflow downloads a card, and the project-cards plugin (`plugins/project-cards` in the
repository) authors cards from Workbench edits.
See [Triage and fix findings](cookbook/fix-findings.md) for the field mapping.

### Model engines

* [AequilibraE](https://www.aequilibrae.com) imports a network with `create_from_gmns` (link, node,
  use_group and geometry tables) and exports with `export_to_gmns`. Validate in the Workbench, then build the
  AequilibraE project from the saved CSV folder.
* [DTALite](https://github.com/asu-trans-ai-lab/DTALite) and [Path4GMNS](https://github.com/jdlph/Path4GMNS)
  read `node.csv` and `link.csv` directly; save as CSV and point them at the folder.
* Commercial packages (Cube, Visum, TransCAD, Emme) generally import GMNS link and node tables through their
  own scripting interfaces rather than a native reader. [What is GMNS?](what-is-gmns.md) explains why the
  spec exists as the common target.

### Builders and notebook maps

[osm2gmns](https://github.com/jiawlu/OSM2GMNS) and `osmnx` build GMNS from OpenStreetMap, as does
[`netstead build`](cookbook/build-from-osm.md). For a quick map inside a notebook without the Workbench,
[View a network on a map](cookbook/view-your-network.md) covers the built-in viewer, and a GeoDataFrame from
`netstead[clean]` drops into lonboard, pydeck or kepler.gl.

## See also

* [Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench](cookbook/workbench.md)
* [Write a Workbench plugin](cookbook/workbench-plugins.md)
* [What is GMNS?](what-is-gmns.md)


<!-- source: roadmap.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/roadmap.md -->

---
title: Status and roadmap
audience: users
kind: concept
summary: What netstead ships today (v1.0 beta), what is being built next, and what is designed but not started.
---

# Status and roadmap

## What it is

A one-page answer to "can I rely on this yet, and what is coming?". It summarizes the design
records that steer the project; those records live in the repository under
[`docs/design/`](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/tree/main/docs/design) and are reviewed like
code, so this page follows them rather than the other way round.

## Why we have it

netstead is in public beta (`1.0.0b2`). The library surface (read, validate, scope, edit) is
stable enough to build on; the Workbench grows by phases, and each phase lands as one pull request.
Knowing which phase is on `main` tells you which cookbook pages apply to the version you installed.

## Mental model

Three layers, maturing at different speeds:

| Layer | Status | Where documented |
|---|---|---|
| **Library** (`netstead.Network`, validation, quality rules, scope, edit with rollback, GeoParquet I/O) | beta, API frozen for v1.0 | [Quickstart](quickstart.md), [Cookbook](cookbook/index.md), [API](reference/api.md) |
| **Builders and surfaces** (OSM and Overture builds, natural-language selection, CLI `--json`, HTTP server, MCP server) | beta | [Build a network](cookbook/build-from-osm.md), [Self-host](cookbook/serve-http.md), [MCP](cookbook/serve-mcp.md) |
| **Workbench** (`netstead app`) and its plugin API | beta; phased; the plugin API is provisional until v1.0 | [Explore in the Workbench](cookbook/workbench.md), [Write a plugin](cookbook/workbench-plugins.md) |

## Shipped

Everything below is on `main` and in the current beta.

- **Library.** DuckDB is the single compute engine (via ibis); pandas, polars and Arrow are
  in/out formats. Geometry is WKB in memory, WKT in CSV and GeoParquet on disk.
- **Builders.** `netstead build` from OpenStreetMap (place, bbox, point and buffer, or a local
  `.osm` file) and from Overture Maps.
- **Natural-language selection.** `netstead select` and the Workbench resolve a phrase such as
  "I-90 EB between Exit 85 and Exit 87" to links, with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or a local Ollama
  model; keys are write-only and nothing leaves the machine unless you opt in.
- **Workbench phases P0 to P3.** Open or import a network (local, URL, OSM, Overture) with
  estimate and approval; linked map and tables with foreign-key navigation; layered settings;
  validation with an issues panel; table edits with live warnings, undo and "save a copy";
  selection verification with pinned anchors, saved selections and export; style, filter and
  navigate actions; the natural-language assistant with approved drafts. Every action is recorded
  and replayable as Python.
- **Plugins.** Python entry-point plugins with a versioned `Host` API (currently 1.7) and
  browser slots for workspaces, panels, commands and map layers.
- **Project cards plugin.** Lives in the repository at `plugins/project-cards` and authors
  [ProjectCards](https://github.com/network-wrangler/projectcard) from Workbench edits: the change
  model, draft cards written as YAML or JSON in Wrangler names, import of card files and of the
  offline edit log, the `project_cards.*` Actions (add a change, undo, commit, import, preview), a
  catalog of cards checked against the open network and applied with a session summary, and the
  Cards panel in the Workbench. See
  [Author ProjectCards in the Workbench](cookbook/workbench-project-cards.md).
- **AI surface.** `--json` on every data command, `llms.txt`, an MCP server with seven tools,
  and Claude Code skills in the repository.

## Being built next

In the order the design records schedule them. None of these are on `main` yet, so no cookbook
page describes them.

1. **Workbench P4: live Python session.** An `app(net)` helper in the top-level package starts the
   Workbench from a notebook on the same `Network` objects, with a handle offering the live selection,
   `show(...)` for temporary layers, `do(action)` and an optional Python console.
2. **Workbench P5: Compare.** `diff_networks(a, b)` and a Compare workspace with added, removed
   and modified features and validation-issue deltas.
3. **Workbench P6: Transit.** A GTFS component beside the roadway network: routes and stops
   layers, transit selections, roadway-to-transit consistency checks.

## Designed, not scheduled

- Applying cards and scenario management inside netstead (builds on the project-cards plugin).
- Cross-linking and export in the data-table view (phase 2 of that scope).
- A nightly performance-regression job for the benchmark suite.
- Interactive geometry editing in the Workbench map (reshaping a link's path, moving a node) —
  beta feedback item 20 from the 2026-10-20 quickstart walk.
- A global filter expression box in the table view, compiled to the same predicate the per-column
  filter popovers use, instead of setting each column separately.
- A GeoLibre plugin that mirrors the Workbench selection; see
  [The Workbench and other tools](workbench-and-other-tools.md).

## How it relates to ...

- The per-release detail is in the [changelog](changelog.md).
- Beta feedback goes through the
  [beta program](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/BETA.md).
- Breaking changes from v0.3 are in the [migration guide](migration/v0.3-to-v1.0.md).

## See also

- [Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench](cookbook/workbench.md)
- [The Workbench and other tools](workbench-and-other-tools.md)
- [What is GMNS?](what-is-gmns.md)

# netstead cookbook

Each recipe is one task, one runnable example, one paragraph of why-it-works. Recipes are intentionally short — for the *design* behind a workflow, follow the "See also" link to the relevant concept page.

For generic Frictionless data-package recipes (S3 reads, format conversion, generic spatial scope), see the [corral cookbook](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/cookbook/).

## Validation + data quality

* [Run validation and read the report](validate-network.md) — interpret severity / category / code.
* [Customize the data-quality rule pack](customize-quality.md) — threshold overrides, disable rules, plug in your own.
* [Triage findings, propose fixes, apply them](fix-findings.md) — propose fixes on individual findings in the viewer, download them as a YAML edit log, replay it in Python.

## Creating networks

* [Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture](build-from-osm.md) — `netstead build --source osm` (needs the `[osm]` extra) or `--source overture` (needs `[overture]`) from a place / bbox / point+buffer.

## Scope + geographic subsetting

* [Build a scope from seed nodes](scope-from-nodes.md) — BFS shortest-path, network buffers, FK pushdown.

For bbox / polygon (non-GMNS-specific) spatial scope, see [corral cookbook: spatial scope](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/cookbook/scope-bbox/).

## Querying + editing linked tables

* [Query and update linked tables](query-and-update.md) — join across foreign keys, inspect lazily (no pandas), edit rows Network-Wrangler-style with rollback.
* [Edit a network with atomic rollback](edit-with-rollback.md) — `Session` lifecycle, dry-run preview, persisted history.

## Surfaces

* [View a network on a map](view-your-network.md) — render a self-contained Leaflet map of any GMNS network, with or without validation overlays.
* [Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench](workbench.md) — linked map + tables, validation with fixes, NL selection, replayable actions.
* [Find links by describing them](find-links.md) — what you can type ("Cedar St between Central Ave and Price Ave", "all residential links"), which requests need a language model, and how fast each is; in the Workbench, `netstead select` or Python.
* [Write a Workbench plugin](workbench-plugins.md) — add Actions, settings, state, routes and a front end as a separate pip package; the `Host` API, trust model, testing and versioning.
* [Author ProjectCards in the Workbench](workbench-project-cards.md) — the project cards plugin: select, change, preview and commit network_wrangler ProjectCards.
* [Run language models locally with Ollama](local-llm-ollama.md) — install Ollama, pull `qwen3:4b`, select in plain English with nothing leaving your machine.
* [Self-host the HTTP server](serve-http.md) — config file, bearer auth, deploying behind a proxy.
* [Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop](serve-mcp.md) — stdio transport, tool list, agent prompts.
* [Run the bundled benchmarks](run-bench.md) — `netstead bench` (load / validate / connectivity timings) and `netstead bench-suite` (create / selection / viz-pack), what to expect on Leavenworth vs regional networks.

## For AI agents specifically

* [Drive both packages from a tool-call loop](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/ai/json-cli/) — every CLI command emits a parseable document with `--json`.
* [AI surface overview](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/ai/) — llms.txt + api-index.json + Skills + MCP.

## Contributing a new recipe

A recipe is `kind: howto` per the [Page Style Guide](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/netstead/docs/_page-style-guide.md) (a contributor page in the repo, not on this site):

* `When to use this` — 1-2 sentences, the trigger.
* `Quick example` — ≤20 lines, copy-pasteable against the Leavenworth fixture, with **prose before the code**.
* `Step-by-step` — numbered, one short paragraph each.
* `Common variations` — collapsible accordions (`???`), one per variation.
* `Pitfalls` — explicit gotchas.
* `See also` — one link per related concept, no diffuse paths.

Open a PR with the new recipe + a link from this index. CI runs every column-0 ```python fence in the docs (`packages/netstead/tests/test_documented_python_contract.py`) and fails if it raises; indented accordion / tab blocks and blocks preceded by `<!-- doctest: skip -->` are not executed, and printed output is not compared.


<!-- source: cookbook/validate-network.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/validate-network.md -->

---
title: Validate a network and read the report
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Run validation against the GMNS spec and interpret the ValidationReport — severity, category, code, and how to filter findings programmatically.
---

# Validate a network and read the report

## When to use this

You have a GMNS network — yours, a vendor's, the output of an edit — and you need to know whether it conforms to the spec before downstream tools (assignment models, AI agents, regulators) touch it. Validation is fast (sub-second on Leavenworth, a few seconds on a regional network) and answers four questions at once: do all required tables exist, do columns match the schema, do foreign keys resolve, and are any of those FKs stale from a recent edit?

## Quick example

Validate the bundled Leavenworth fixture from the shell. Add `--json` to any `netstead` (or `corral`) CLI command and the output becomes a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout — pipe into `jq`, save to a file, feed to a script or AI agent. Default output is human-readable rich panels.

```bash
netstead validate --json packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
```

Expected — the command exits 0 because Leavenworth has no ERRORs. The issue list holds 16 INFO entries (`structural.missing_optional_resource`, one per optional GMNS table the fixture doesn't ship) and nothing else. (`node` declares a foreign key into `zone`, but the fixture has no `node.zone_id` column, so there is nothing to verify and no finding is raised.)

```json
{"header": "validation report: ...", "issues": [{"severity": "info", "code": "structural.missing_optional_resource", ...}, ...]}
```

The same call from Python returns a `ValidationReport` dataclass:

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
report = net.validate()
print(f"is_clean={report.is_clean}  issues={len(report.issues)}")
```

Expected:

```text
is_clean=True  issues=16
```

`is_clean` is `True` because no ERROR or WARNING fired; the INFO findings don't break it. `report.has_errors` is `False`.

The CLI exits non-zero if any ERROR-severity finding fires, so it drops straight into a CI gate.

![Validation report card for the Leavenworth fixture](../assets/screenshots/leavenworth-validation-report.png){ .screenshot }
*Validation report card. Zero ERRORs, zero WARNINGs, and 16 INFO findings for the optional tables the fixture doesn't ship. Data-quality rules are a separate pass (`netstead quality`) and don't appear here.*

## Step-by-step

### 1. Run validation

`net.validate()` runs all four passes — structural, schema, FK, sync-state — and returns a `ValidationReport`. Toggle individual passes with boolean kwargs:

```python
report = net.validate()                                                  # all four passes
report = net.validate(structural=False, sync_state=False)                # schema + FK only
```

The same operation is available from the shell, with three output formats:

```bash
netstead validate <source>                       # human-readable summary
netstead validate <source> --all                 # ...one row per finding, nothing folded
netstead validate <source> --json                # machine-readable
netstead validate <source> --html report.html    # standalone HTML report
```

The human-readable table opens with a severity summary line (`0 errors · 1 warning · 16 info`)
and names the source once. Structural findings that differ only by resource — the sixteen
`structural.missing_optional_resource` lines above — fold into one row whose table column reads
`16 tables` and whose message lists the absent resources; `--all` expands them to a row each.
`--json` is never folded.

### 2. Read the report shape

`ValidationReport` is a dataclass with five fields and properties you'll touch:

| Field / property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `report.is_clean` | `bool` | `True` iff no ERROR **and** no WARNING fired. INFO findings don't break it. |
| `report.has_errors` | `bool` | `True` iff ≥1 ERROR-severity issue fired. CI gates usually want `if report.has_errors:`. |
| `report.has_warnings` | `bool` | `True` iff ≥1 WARNING-severity issue fired. |
| `report.spec_version` | `str` | The GMNS spec version the validator ran against. |
| `report.issues` | `list[Issue]` | One entry per finding. |

Each `Issue` is a small dataclass carrying severity, category, a stable code, a human-readable message, and the offending row coordinates when known:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
@dataclass
class Issue:
    severity: Severity      # ERROR | WARNING | INFO
    category: Category      # SCHEMA | STRUCTURAL | FOREIGN_KEY | SYNC_STATE | DATA_QUALITY
    code: str               # stable identifier, e.g. "schema.required"
    message: str            # human-readable
    table: str | None       # table the finding is about
    column: str | None      # column, if applicable
    row: int | None         # row index, if applicable
    fix_hint: str | None    # what to do about it
    extra: dict             # adapter-specific payload (FK target, coordinates, ...)
```

### 3. Filter by severity

Most CI gates want `if errors: sys.exit(1)`. The CLI does this for you; from Python it's a one-liner:

```python
from corral.validation import Severity

errors = [i for i in report.issues if i.severity is Severity.ERROR]
warnings = [i for i in report.issues if i.severity is Severity.WARNING]
```

### 4. Filter by category

Categories group findings by which validation pass produced them:

```python
from corral.validation import Category

schema_problems = [i for i in report.issues if i.category is Category.SCHEMA]
fk_problems = [i for i in report.issues if i.category is Category.FOREIGN_KEY]
```

* `SCHEMA` — field-level type / enum / required-column violations.
* `STRUCTURAL` — package-level shape problems (missing required table, missing required file).
* `FOREIGN_KEY` — cross-table integrity (`link.from_node_id` points at a node that doesn't exist).
* `SYNC_STATE` — FKs that resolved on disk but were invalidated by an in-memory edit (see [edit-with-rollback](edit-with-rollback.md)).
* `DATA_QUALITY` — rule-pack findings (high-speed-residential, lane-count-mismatch, etc.). Always WARNING / INFO; see [customize the quality pack](customize-quality.md).

### 5. Common codes you'll see

Stable identifier strings let you script around specific findings without parsing free-text messages. Codes live inline at the top of each validator module (see [`corral.validation.structural`](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/corral/corral/validation/structural.py), [`schema_check`](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/corral/corral/validation/schema_check.py), [`foreign_keys`](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/corral/corral/validation/foreign_keys.py), [`sync_state`](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/corral/corral/validation/sync_state.py)). The most common ones:

| Code | Category | Severity | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema.required` | SCHEMA | ERROR | A required column is missing or null on a row. |
| `schema.enum` | SCHEMA | ERROR | A column value isn't in the spec-defined enum set. |
| `schema.type` | SCHEMA | ERROR | A value doesn't parse as the declared type. |
| `structural.missing_required_resource` | STRUCTURAL | ERROR | A required table (`link`, `node`) isn't in the package. |
| `structural.missing_optional_resource` | STRUCTURAL | INFO | An optional spec table isn't in the package. Leavenworth reports 16 of these. |
| `structural.missing_file` | STRUCTURAL | ERROR | A table is declared in the package descriptor but the file isn't there. |
| `fk.missing_target` | FOREIGN_KEY | ERROR | FK points at a row that doesn't exist in the parent table. |
| `fk.null_in_required_fk` | FOREIGN_KEY | ERROR | A required FK column is null on a row. |
| `fk.unverifiable` | FOREIGN_KEY | WARNING | The FK's target table isn't in the package, so it can't be checked and the source column holds at least one value. An absent or all-null source column raises nothing. |
| `sync.fk_stale` | SYNC_STATE | ERROR | An edit invalidated an FK and no `recompute` ran. |
| `quality.high_speed_residential` | DATA_QUALITY | WARNING | Residential link with speed limit above the configured threshold. |

## Common variations

???+ note "Default — full validation, rich console output"
    The most common path: run all four passes and read the panel.

    ```bash
    netstead validate <source>
    ```

??? note "JSON for scripts and AI agents"
    `--json` emits one parseable document on stdout — exits non-zero on ERROR.

    ```bash
    netstead validate <source> --json | jq '.issues[] | select(.severity=="error")'
    ```

??? note "Interactive map+table HTML report (`--html`)"
    Self-contained file you can email or upload to a docs site. The map
    pane on top plots each finding on the actual network geometry
    (Leaflet, vendored — no network calls when the report is opened);
    the filterable table below shows the same findings with severity,
    code, message, and fix hint. A "Resources" table above the findings
    lists every spec table with required / optional, present ✓ / ✗ and
    its row count, and the "Unlocated findings" block (collapsed by
    default) folds repeated structural findings into one line. For
    networks imported from OpenStreetMap, each finding's popup carries
    a one-click "Edit in OSM" deep link to the iD editor.

    ```bash
    netstead validate <source> --html report.html
    ```

    Or programmatically:

    ```python
    from netstead.map import render_validation_html
    open("report.html", "w").write(render_validation_html(net, report))
    ```

    Requires `pip install 'netstead[reports]'`. When that extra is not
    installed, `--html` still writes a file — the older corral
    table-only HTML — and prints a stderr note pointing at the install
    command.

??? note "Findings spreadsheet (`--csv` / `--xlsx`)"
    Flat one-row-per-finding spreadsheet — the right shape for triage in
    Excel, Google Sheets, or jq.

    ```bash
    netstead validate <source> --csv findings.csv --xlsx findings.xlsx
    ```

    Columns: `severity, category, code, table, column, row, message,
    fix_hint, extra`. The `extra` column is a JSON blob carrying
    adapter-specific payload (FK target, OSM provenance, …).
    `--xlsx` needs `[reports]`; `--csv` works on the lean install.

??? note "Just the failing tables"
    Useful for triaging which datasets need attention first.

    ```python
    from corral.reports import Severity
    failing = {i.table for i in report.issues if i.severity is Severity.ERROR}
    ```

??? note "Embed in a CI step"
    Non-zero exit code on ERROR — no extra wiring needed.

    ```bash
    netstead validate ./data || exit 1
    ```

??? note "Pretty-print in a notebook"
    `ValidationReport` ships a `_repr_html_`; just leave it as the last cell expression.

    ```python
    report  # renders an HTML summary in Jupyter
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **WARNING-level findings don't fail CI.** That's intentional — data-quality findings are advisory. If you want them to be blocking, post-process: `if any(i.code.startswith("quality.") for i in report.issues): sys.exit(1)`.
* **Data-quality thresholds are configurable.** A WARNING firing on your network may just mean the default threshold doesn't match your context (e.g. metric vs imperial speed). See the [customize the quality pack](customize-quality.md) recipe.
* **`sync.fk_stale` only fires after an edit.** A freshly-loaded package can't be out of sync with itself. If you see this in CI, an upstream step in the same process mutated the network.
* **The validator runs against the spec version embedded in the package.** Override with `Network.from_source(path, spec_version="0.96")` if the package is mislabeled.

## See also

* [Architecture](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/architecture/) — the four-pass validator design.
* [Edit with rollback](edit-with-rollback.md) — `sync.fk_stale` is produced by edits without a `recompute_fks`.
* [API reference](../reference/api.md) — `ValidationReport`, `Issue`, `Severity`, `Category`.


<!-- source: cookbook/customize-quality.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/customize-quality.md -->

---
title: Customize the data-quality rule pack
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Override thresholds, disable rules, promote severity, and register your own rule via entry point.
---

# Customize the data-quality rule pack

## When to use this

GMNS defaults are designed for typical mid-sized urban networks. Override them when:

* Your network's speed limits, lane counts, or geometry tolerances differ from the defaults (a 30 mph residential cap, or a CRS in degrees instead of meters).
* You want to silence a rule that's noise on your data.
* You want to plug in a project-specific quality rule.

## Quick example

Raise the residential-speed threshold from the default 35 mph to 45 mph. `RuleConfig.thresholds` merges into the rule's defaults — you only specify the keys you want to change. Every residential link in Leavenworth is posted at 40 mph, so the default fires 271 warnings and 45 mph silences all of them:

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.quality import run_quality, RuleConfig

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
default = run_quality(net)
relaxed = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 45.0})},
)
print(f"{len(default.issues)} issues at 35 mph, {len(relaxed.issues)} at 45 mph")
```

Expected:

```text
271 issues at 35 mph, 0 at 45 mph
```

![Quality report card for the Leavenworth fixture](../assets/screenshots/leavenworth-quality-report.png){ .screenshot }
*Quality report card at the default thresholds: 271 `quality.high_speed_residential` WARNINGs, one per residential link posted at 40 mph. Raising `speed_limit_mph` to 45 silences them all; lowering it to 30 changes nothing, because no residential link sits between 30 and 35 mph.*

## Step-by-step

### 1. List the rules currently registered

Inspect the registered rule pack to see codes, defaults, and severities. The GMNS pack ships nine rules out of the box:

```python
from corral.quality import list_rules, get_rule
from netstead.quality import register_all

register_all()                                   # populate the registry
for code in list_rules():
    rule = get_rule(code)
    print(f"{rule.code:42} {rule.severity.value:8} {rule.description[:50]}")
```

| Code | Threshold key | Default | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| `quality.high_speed_residential` | `speed_limit_mph` | `35` | WARNING |
| `quality.disconnected_components` | (no threshold) | — | INFO |
| `quality.lane_count_mismatch` | (no threshold) | — | WARNING |
| `quality.duplicate_near_nodes` | `epsilon_units` | `1e-5` | WARNING |
| `quality.sharp_angle_bends` | `min_angle_degrees` | `30` | WARNING |
| `quality.implausible_vc` | `vc_max` | `1.5` | WARNING |
| `quality.missing_critical_fields` | `coverage_min` | `0.90` | INFO |
| `quality.non_unique_combination` | `combinations` | see below | WARNING |
| `quality.overlapping_links` | `min_overlap_units` | `0` | WARNING |

Three of these are conditional: `quality.disconnected_components` builds the scipy graph index, so `run_quality` needs the `[graph]` extra; `quality.overlapping_links` needs shapely (the `[clean]` extra) and link shapes, inline or in the `geometry` table; `quality.sharp_angle_bends` only applies when the link table carries an inline `geometry` column (Leavenworth keeps geometry in a separate table, so the rule is skipped there).

`quality.non_unique_combination` catches rows that repeat a column combination GMNS expects to be unique even though the table's primary key is a surrogate id: two `link_tod` rows for the same `link_id` and `time_day` pass spec validation but contradict each other. It emits one issue per repeated combination, with the row positions in `extra["rows"]`. By default it checks `(<parent id>, time_day)` and `(<parent id>, timeday_id)` on every time-of-day table (`link_tod`, `lane_tod`, `segment_tod`, `segment_lane_tod`, `movement_tod`, `signal_timing_plan`), plus `(link_id, lane_num)` on `lane`, `(segment_id, lane_num)` on `segment_lane` and `(timing_plan_id, signal_phase_num)` on `signal_timing_phase` (read-only, as `netstead.quality.DEFAULT_UNIQUE_COMBINATIONS`). Setting `combinations` replaces that list, so name every combination you still want. A configured combination whose table or columns the network lacks is logged as a warning on the `netstead.quality.rules` logger (probably a typo). It is deliberately not an issue: `severity_override` applies to every issue a rule emits, so promoting this rule to ERROR in CI fails only on real duplicates, never on a network that lacks an optional table. A value that is not a mapping of table name to lists of column names raises `ValueError`, and the Workbench rejects it (and a negative `epsilon_units`) when the setting is saved:

```python
report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={
        "quality.non_unique_combination": RuleConfig(
            thresholds={"combinations": {"link_tod": [["link_id", "time_day"]], "link": [["osm_way_id", "from_node_id"]]}}
        )
    },
)
```

### 2. Override a threshold

`RuleConfig.thresholds` is merged into the rule's defaults — you only specify the keys you want to change. Override multiple rules in one call:

```python
report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={
        "quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 25.0}),
        "quality.sharp_angle_bends": RuleConfig(thresholds={"min_angle_degrees": 45.0}),
    },
)
```

The Workbench applies the same per-rule configuration from its `validation.rules` setting (Settings → Validation, keyed by rule code) — see [Validate and fix in the Workbench](workbench.md#validate-and-fix).

### 3. Disable a rule entirely

A disabled rule produces no issues and isn't listed in the report:

```python
report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.missing_critical_fields": RuleConfig(enabled=False)},
)
```

### 4. Promote (or demote) severity

A common case: your CI pipeline should fail on lane-count mismatches even though the rule ships as WARNING. Use `severity_override` to promote, then check `report.issues` and exit non-zero accordingly:

```python
import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from corral.quality import RuleConfig, run_quality
from corral.reports import Severity

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
report = run_quality(
    net,
    config={"quality.lane_count_mismatch": RuleConfig(severity_override=Severity.ERROR)},
)
has_errors = any(i.severity is Severity.ERROR for i in report.issues)
# In a CI script: sys.exit(1 if has_errors else 0)
```

### 5. Write your own rule and register it

A rule is a plain class (no base class needed — `corral.quality.Rule` is a `Protocol`) with three attributes, `code`, `description` and `severity`, and two methods: `applies_to(package) -> bool`, a cheap predicate the runner calls first, and `run(package, report, config)`, which appends findings to `report` with `report.add_issue(...)`. Accept the third `config` argument to read `RuleConfig.thresholds`; a rule with no thresholds may define `run(self, package, report)` and the runner passes two arguments. Don't apply `severity_override` yourself — `run_quality` rewrites the severity of every issue your rule emitted after it returns.

Write the predicate against the table's ibis expression (`package.tables["link"].expr`) so DuckDB filters the rows and only the offending ones reach Python; on a 200k-link network that is the difference between materializing every row and fetching a handful. Number the rows with `ibis.row_number()` *before* filtering so `Issue.row` is the row's position in the whole table. This rule flags links longer than a configurable maximum (Leavenworth's `length` column is in metres):

```python
import ibis
from corral.quality import RuleConfig, register_rule, run_quality
from corral.reports import Category, Issue, Severity


class LongLinkRule:
    code = "quality.long_link"
    description = "Link longer than the configured maximum length."
    severity = Severity.WARNING

    def applies_to(self, package) -> bool:
        link = package.tables.get("link")
        return link is not None and {"link_id", "length"} <= set(link.columns())

    def run(self, package, report, config: RuleConfig | None = None) -> None:
        thresholds = config.thresholds if config else {}
        max_length = float(thresholds.get("max_length", 1000.0))
        link = package.tables["link"].expr
        link = link.mutate(row=ibis.row_number())
        offending = (
            link.filter(link.length.notnull(), link.length > max_length)
            .select("row", "link_id", "length")
            .order_by("row")
        )
        for row in offending.to_pyarrow().to_pylist():
            report.add_issue(
                Issue(
                    severity=self.severity,
                    category=Category.DATA_QUALITY,
                    code=self.code,
                    message=f"link {row['link_id']} is {row['length']:.0f} long (> {max_length:.0f})",
                    table="link",
                    column="length",
                    row=row["row"],
                    fix_hint="Split the link, or check its length.",
                )
            )


register_rule(LongLinkRule())
report = run_quality(net, config={"quality.long_link": RuleConfig(thresholds={"max_length": 500.0})})
print(sum(1 for i in report.issues if i.code == "quality.long_link"), "links over 500 m")
```

Expected:

```text
4 links over 500 m
```

To ship the rule with a package, expose a **zero-argument factory that returns `list[Rule]`** and declare it under the `corral.quality.rules` entry point in your `pyproject.toml`. `run_quality` loads every entry point on its first call and registers each returned rule — this is exactly how netstead registers its own pack (`netstead.quality:register_all`):

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
# myproject/rules.py
def register_rules() -> list:
    return [LongLinkRule()]
```

```toml
[project.entry-points."corral.quality.rules"]
myproject = "myproject.rules:register_rules"
```

## Common variations

???+ note "Default — override one threshold for one run"
    Most common pattern: tighten or loosen a single threshold without touching anything else.

    ```python
    report = run_quality(
        net,
        config={"quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 30.0})},
    )
    ```

??? note "Silence a noisy rule entirely"
    Disable it via `RuleConfig(enabled=False)`; the rule contributes no issues and doesn't appear in the report.

    ```python
    report = run_quality(net, config={"quality.missing_critical_fields": RuleConfig(enabled=False)})
    ```

??? note "Promote a WARNING to ERROR for CI"
    Use `severity_override`; then exit non-zero if any ERROR issue appears.

    ```python
    report = run_quality(
        net,
        config={"quality.lane_count_mismatch": RuleConfig(severity_override=Severity.ERROR)},
    )
    ```

??? note "Ship a custom rule with your package"
    Point the `corral.quality.rules` entry point at a zero-argument callable that returns your rule instances; `run_quality` discovers and registers them on first call.

    ```toml
    [project.entry-points."corral.quality.rules"]
    myproject = "myproject.rules:register_rules"
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **`epsilon_units` is CRS-sensitive.** The default `1e-5` is tight for WGS84 degrees (~1 metre near the equator). A network in projected meters needs something like `epsilon_units=0.5` for the same intent. Always set this explicitly for non-WGS84 networks.
* **`quality.overlapping_links` measures overlap in CRS units too.** It flags two links whose shapes share a stretch longer than `min_overlap_units` (default `0`, so any shared stretch). Links that only meet at a node, cross, or carry the identical shape (the usual way two directions of a two-way street are drawn) are not flagged; a short link running along part of a longer one is. Raise `min_overlap_units` to ignore short shared stretches, e.g. `0.00002` (about 2 m) in WGS84 degrees or `2.0` in projected metres.
* **`quality.overlapping_links` matches exactly, with no tolerance.** Only segments the two shapes share exactly are caught; two digitisations of the same road a hair apart, or whose vertices never line up on a common segment, are not flagged, and `min_overlap_units` does not widen the match. It can also get slow when many link bounding boxes overlap with real area, as long or diagonal links in WGS84 do; disable it with `RuleConfig(enabled=False)` if it dominates a run.
* **`epsilon_units` must not be negative.** `quality.duplicate_near_nodes` raises `ValueError` for a negative value; `0` flags only exact duplicates.
* **`severity_override` doesn't mute — it replaces.** Setting `severity_override=Severity.INFO` on a WARNING rule still produces issues; if you want to drop them, use `enabled=False`.
* **`applies_to` is a method, not a tuple.** The runner calls `rule.applies_to(package)` before `run` and skips the rule silently when it returns `False`. Check for the tables and columns you need there (a rule reading `signal` should return `False` when the table is absent) rather than raising inside `run`.

## See also

* [Quickstart](../quickstart.md#4-run-data-quality-checks) — the default quality flow.
* [API reference](../reference/api.md) — `run_quality`, `RuleConfig`, `Rule`, `Issue`.


<!-- source: cookbook/fix-findings.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/fix-findings.md -->

---
title: Triage findings, propose fixes, apply them
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Use the interactive viewer to propose fixes on individual validation findings, download them as a YAML edit log, and replay the log against your network in Python — with overwrite or save-as.
---

# Triage findings, propose fixes, apply them

## When to use this

You ran `netstead validate` and you have findings to address. You want to
triage them visually, propose fixes one at a time without writing
Python for each, then apply them deterministically and save. The flow
splits cleanly into two halves:

1. **Browser** — open the HTML report, click each finding's "Propose
   fix" button, accumulate an edit log.
2. **Python** — load the log, replay it against your network, save
   (overwrite or save-as).

The split lets you triage clickwise but always end up with a structured,
replay-able record of what changed.

## Quick example

```bash
# 1. Generate the validation report
uv run netstead validate ./my-net --html /tmp/report.html
open /tmp/report.html
```

In the browser:

- Each finding marker → click → popup with `Propose fix` button
- Click `Propose fix` → inline editor with the column pre-filled and
  the current value loaded → enter new value + reason → `Add to edit log`
- Bottom-right floating sidebar tracks your edits — `Download YAML`
  when done

Then back in Python:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.map.edits import apply_edits, load_edit_log

net = Network.from_source("./my-net")
log = load_edit_log("/path/to/edits-2026-06-30T19-00-00.yaml")
result = apply_edits(net, log)

print(result.summary())                # "12 applied, 2 skipped"
for s in result.skipped:               # inspect anything that didn't apply
    print(s.edit.id, "→", s.reason)

# Save either way — Network.write() takes a destination path. The format is
# inferred from the extension; a bare directory name writes Parquet, so pass
# format="csv" when you want to keep a CSV package.
result.net.write("./my-net", format="csv", overwrite=True)   # overwrite the CSV source
result.net.write("./my-net-v2")                              # new directory, Parquet
```

## The edit log shape

The download is a [network-wrangler ProjectCard](https://network-wrangler.github.io/projectcard/main/json-schemas/):
one card per session, with a top-level `changes:` array of
`roadway_property_change` entries. Each fix targets a single row via its
primary key (not positional row index — PKs survive row reordering
and partial reloads):

```yaml
project: netstead edits 2026-06-30T19:00:00.000Z
tags: [netstead, edit-log]
notes: |
  created_at: 2026-06-30T19:00:00.000Z
  client: netstead.map (browser)
  netstead.note[0]: schema.required: free_speed missing · issue_id=i0 · edit_id=el7f9c3a
changes:
  - roadway_property_change:
      facility:
        links:
          model_link_id: [42]
          ignore_missing: false     # a clicked id (see below for what a missing link 42 does)
      property_changes:
        free_speed:
          existing: 40              # netstead "from" — drift check on apply
          set: 25                   # netstead "to"
```

**Interop with network-wrangler.** The file is a schema-valid
ProjectCard; you can pipe it into network-wrangler's own tooling or
import it with the [project cards plugin](workbench-project-cards.md).
GMNS `link_id` maps to `model_link_id` under the facility's `links`
(`node_id` to `model_node_id` under `nodes`), with
`ignore_missing: false` because the ids were clicked. When a listed
link is gone, network-wrangler and the project cards plugin refuse the
change; netstead's own `apply_edits` skips that edit and reports it in
`result.skipped` (see [Pitfalls](#pitfalls)). Per-cell values
live under `property_changes.<column>.set` with an optional `existing`
drift check. A change cannot carry its own notes, so each fix's
reason, issue id and edit id are one `netstead.note[<i>]:` line of the
card's `notes`, where `<i>` is the change's position in `changes`.
`load_edit_log` still reads logs written before this shape (ids at the
top of the facility, a `notes` on each change).

`existing:` is the value the browser-side editor *thought* was there
when you proposed the fix. `apply_edits` uses it for a drift check —
if the table's current value differs, the edit is skipped (with a
reason) rather than silently clobbering a concurrent change. Omit
`existing:` (or send `null`) to disable the check.

## Variations

??? note "Pass the log to a colleague (review workflow)"
    Don't apply anything locally. Download the YAML, email it (or open
    a PR with it). They run `apply_edits` against their copy of the
    network when they're ready.

??? note "Replay against a newer version of the same network"
    The vendor sent you v2 of the network. Run `apply_edits(v2_net, log)`
    — every edit whose PK still exists and whose `existing:` still matches
    applies cleanly. Anything that drifted shows up in `result.skipped`
    with a precise reason.

??? note "Bulk fixes from Python"
    `Edit` is a plain dataclass — build a `list[Edit]` programmatically
    ("every residential link with free_speed > 25 should be set to 25"),
    wrap it in an `EditLog`, and apply with the same `apply_edits` path.
    No browser needed. `pk` is a dict of primary-key columns, `to_value`
    the new cell value; `from_value` is optional and turns on the drift check.

    ```python
    import netstead
    from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
    from netstead.map.edits import Edit, EditLog, apply_edits

    net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
    links = net.links.to_pandas()
    too_fast = links[(links.facility_type == "residential") & (links.free_speed > 25)].link_id

    edits = [
        Edit(id=f"cap-{lid}", kind="fix", table="link", pk={"link_id": int(lid)},
             column="free_speed", to_value=25.0, reason="residential cap")
        for lid in too_fast
    ]
    result = apply_edits(net, EditLog(edits=edits))
    print(result.summary())   # "271 applied, 0 skipped" on Leavenworth
    ```

??? note "Clear the log mid-session"
    The browser persists edits in `sessionStorage`. A page refresh
    keeps them. The sidebar's `Clear` button drops them (with a confirm
    prompt).

## Pitfalls

- **The browser-side log is per-session.** It lives in `sessionStorage`,
  so opening the report in a different tab gives you a fresh log. Always
  Download YAML before closing the tab if you want to keep the work.
- **Edits identify rows by PK, not row index.** That's deliberate — row
  index isn't stable across reloads. If your edit log targets
  `facility: {links: {model_link_id: [42], ignore_missing: false}}` and link_id 42 no longer exists in the
  destination network, `apply_edits` skips that edit and reports it in
  `result.skipped` as `pk {'link_id': 42} not found in 'link'` (whatever
  `ignore_missing` says). network-wrangler and the project cards plugin
  follow `ignore_missing: false` and refuse the change instead.
- **Drift checks compare values pre-cast.** When the source column is a
  number, the editor coerces the new value to a number too. When in
  doubt, look at the YAML — `existing: 40` vs `existing: '40'` matter for
  the strict drift check (only null and NaN are treated as the same
  "missing" value).

## See also

* [View a network on a map](view-your-network.md) — the embedding the
  edit-log UI lives on top of.
* [Validate a network](validate-network.md) — produces the findings the
  Propose-fix flow targets.
* `netstead.map.NetworkMap` — the embeddable component itself.


<!-- source: cookbook/build-from-osm.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/build-from-osm.md -->

---
title: Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: netstead build turns an area into a validated GMNS node + link network from OpenStreetMap (Overpass) or Overture Maps (GeoParquet), from the CLI or Python.
---

# Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture

## When to use this

You need a GMNS network for a study area and don't have one yet. Point `netstead` at a place name, a bounding box, or a lat/lon + buffer and it fetches the road network — from OpenStreetMap via Overpass (`--source osm`, the default) or from Overture Maps' transportation theme (`--source overture`) — and writes a validated GMNS `node` + `link` package. No `osmnx` or `osm2gmns` required.

Requires the matching optional extra: `pip install 'netstead[osm]'` or `pip install 'netstead[overture]'`.

## Quick example

Build the drivable network for a place and write it as CSV. The area is geocoded via Nominatim, the road network is fetched from Overpass, and the result is a GMNS package on disk:

```bash
netstead build --place "Leavenworth, WA" --network-type roads --source osm --format csv ./leavenworth-osm
```

The command prints a summary (`nodes`, `links`, `spec_version`); add `--json` for a machine-readable document.

## Step-by-step

### 1. Install the extra

```bash
pip install 'netstead[osm]'        # --source osm (default)
pip install 'netstead[overture]'   # --source overture
```

Overture is read as GeoParquet straight through corral's bundled DuckDB, so `[overture]` adds only the mapping-data loader. Geocoding a `--place` string uses Nominatim from the `[osm]` extra, so an Overture build by place name needs both.

### 2. Pick how you specify the area

One of three, mutually exclusive:

```bash
# A place name (city / county / neighborhood) — geocoded to a boundary polygon.
netstead build --place "Leavenworth, WA" ./net

# A bounding box: west,south,east,north (EPSG:4326).
netstead build --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 ./net

# A point (lat,lon) plus a buffer in metres.
netstead build --point 47.596,-120.66 --buffer 800 ./net
```

### 3. Choose the source

`--source osm` (the default) fetches from Overpass. `--source overture` reads the pinned Overture release from cloud GeoParquet; `--overture-release` moves the pin and `--data-root` points at an alternative base URI or a local snapshot directory holding `segment.parquet` / `connector.parquet`. Both flags are rejected with `--source osm`:

```bash
netstead build --source overture --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 ./leavenworth-overture
netstead build --source overture --overture-release 2026-09-23.1 --data-root /data/overture-snapshot --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 ./net
```

### 4. Choose modes and output format

`--network-type` is `roads` (motorway through residential, service and other roads, links and busways), `paths` (footways, paths, pedestrian ways, steps, tracks, cycleways and bridleways), or both: repeat the option or comma-separate (`--network-type roads,paths`). Proposed, construction and corridor ways are never built. The old names still work but are deprecated: `drive` means `roads`; `walk`, `bike` and `all` mean `roads,paths`. Overture builds use the same two types, mapped onto Overture road classes (no busway class exists there). The output format is inferred from the destination extension, or set it explicitly with `--format` (`csv` / `parquet` / `duckdb` / `zip`). A destination with no extension — `./net` in the examples above — is written as a **Parquet** directory; pass `--format csv` for CSV:

```bash
netstead build --place "Leavenworth, WA" --network-type roads,paths --format parquet ./full-net
```

### 5. Validate what you built

The build already produces a schema-valid package; run `netstead validate` any time to confirm and to see the report:

```bash
netstead validate ./leavenworth-osm
```

## Python API

Programmatic equivalent — `netstead.osm.build_network_from_osm` returns a `Network` (a `corral` package) you can validate, scope, or write. The area is a place string, a `(lat, lon)` point with `buffer_m`, or a `(west, south, east, north)` bbox:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead.osm import build_network_from_osm

net = build_network_from_osm("Leavenworth, WA", network_type="roads")
print(net.links.count(), net.nodes.count())
net.write("leavenworth-osm", format="csv", overwrite=True)
```

`netstead.overture.build_network_from_overture` has the same shape, plus `overture_release` (the pinned release string) and `data_root` (alternative base URI or local snapshot directory). Its `extra_tags` are Overture segment property paths (e.g. `"subclass"`, `"road_surface"`) rather than OSM tag keys:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead.overture import build_network_from_overture

net = build_network_from_overture((-120.67, 47.58, -120.64, 47.61), network_type="roads")
net.write("leavenworth-overture")   # no extension → Parquet directory
```

If you already have node/link records (e.g. from your own fetch, or to benchmark the build path without the network), assemble a `Network` directly with `netstead.osm.network_from_records`:

```python
from netstead.osm import network_from_records

nodes = [
    {"node_id": 1, "x_coord": -120.66, "y_coord": 47.60},
    {"node_id": 2, "x_coord": -120.65, "y_coord": 47.60},
]
links = [
    {"link_id": 1, "from_node_id": 1, "to_node_id": 2, "directed": True,
     "facility_type": "residential", "geometry": "LINESTRING (-120.66 47.6, -120.65 47.6)"},
    {"link_id": 2, "from_node_id": 2, "to_node_id": 1, "directed": True,
     "facility_type": "residential", "geometry": "LINESTRING (-120.65 47.6, -120.66 47.6)"},
]
net = network_from_records(nodes, links)
print(net.links.count())
```

## How the conversion works

* **Topology.** A GMNS node is created at every OSM intersection (a node shared by two or more ways) and at each way's endpoints. Intermediate shape points are dropped as nodes and kept as the link's WKT geometry; their OSM ids are retained on the link's `osm_node_ids` column for provenance, alongside `osm_way_id`.
* **Direction.** Every link is `directed=True`. A two-way street becomes **two** directed links (one per direction); a oneway street becomes one, honoring `oneway=-1` and implied-oneway (motorways, roundabouts).
* **Attributes.** `name`, `lanes`, `free_speed`, and `facility_type` are mapped from OSM tags via the maintained data file `netstead/osm/mappings/osm_to_gmns.yaml`. Pass `--extra-tags surface,bridge` (or `extra_tags=[...]`) to carry additional OSM tags through as extra columns. Edit the YAML to change or extend the mapping — no code change needed.

## Common variations

???+ note "Point + buffer"
    A circle of road around a coordinate (metres).

    ```bash
    netstead build --point 47.596,-120.66 --buffer 800 ./net
    ```

??? note "Carry extra OSM tags"
    Add columns to the link table verbatim.

    ```bash
    netstead build --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 --extra-tags surface,bridge ./net
    ```

??? note "Build from a local .osm XML or Overpass JSON file"
    No network access: `build_network_from_osm_file` reads an `.osm` XML file or an Overpass `[out:json]` export (`.json`) and applies the same `network_type` filter and tag mapping. It is Python-only (no `netstead build` flag) and still needs the `[osm]` extra for the mapping loader.

    <!-- doctest: skip -->
    ```python
    from netstead.osm import build_network_from_osm_file

    net = build_network_from_osm_file("leavenworth.osm", network_type="roads", extra_tags=["surface"])
    net.write("leavenworth-osm", format="csv")
    ```

??? note "Build from Overture Maps"
    Same area options; swap the source. Overture link geometry comes from segment shapes and nodes from Overture connectors.

    ```bash
    netstead build --source overture --bbox -120.67,47.58,-120.64,47.61 --format csv ./leavenworth-overture
    ```

??? note "Benchmark the build"
    The `scripts/bench_osm_build.py` harness times the convert + build path (DuckDB is the single compute engine); add `--baselines` for directional osmnx / osm2gmns comparisons.

    ```bash
    uv run python scripts/bench_osm_build.py --grids 10,40,120 --json
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **Units.** GMNS is unit-agnostic — units are declared per-dataset, so the build writes a `config` table stating them: `free_speed` is **mph** (faithful to US OSM `maxspeed` tags; unit-less values are treated as km/h and converted), `length` is geodesic **metres**, `crs` is `EPSG:4326`. Re-unit downstream if your convention differs.
* **Overpass limits.** The public Overpass endpoint rate-limits and times out on large areas. For regional extracts (e.g. a metro), point at a self-hosted endpoint (`endpoint=` in the Python API) rather than hammering the public server.
* **Nominatim policy.** Place-name geocoding uses the public Nominatim, which is not for bulk/automated use. Prefer `--bbox` for scripted/repeated runs.
* **Attribution.** OSM data is ODbL-licensed — attribute OpenStreetMap in anything you publish from these networks. Overture data is ODbL too: derived products must credit "© OpenStreetMap contributors, © Overture Maps Foundation" (see [Overture's attribution page](https://docs.overturemaps.org/attribution/)); netstead reads Overture data and does not redistribute it.
* **`netstead[osm]` / `netstead[overture]` required.** Without the matching extra the command exits with an install hint.

## See also

* [Run validation and read the report](validate-network.md) — interpret the report from `netstead validate`.
* [Run the bundled benchmarks](run-bench.md) — `netstead bench` for load/validate timings on an existing network.


<!-- source: cookbook/scope-from-nodes.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/scope-from-nodes.md -->

---
title: Build a scope from seed nodes
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Network-aware scope from a list of node ids — BFS path-between, FK pushdown, chainable set ops.
---

# Build a scope from seed nodes

## When to use this

You have a list of node ids (e.g. study-area boundary nodes, signalised intersections, a corridor's endpoints) and want the subgraph that connects them — every link on a shortest path, every dependent `lane` / `link_tod` / `signal_*` row, with foreign keys pre-filtered.

## Quick example

Build a scope from three seed nodes. With `path_between=True` (the default), BFS shortest paths between every pair of seeds determine what's included; `.apply()` materializes the result as a normal `Network`:

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
sub = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True).apply()
print(f"scoped: {sub.links.count()} links, {sub.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

Expected:

```text
scoped: 28 links, 14 nodes
```

![Scoped Leavenworth subnetwork rendered on a folium map](../assets/screenshots/leavenworth-scoped-map.png){ .screenshot }
*The scope from seed nodes 1, 25, and 50. Shortest paths between the seeds determine which interior links are kept; every dependent `lane`, `link_tod`, and signal row is FK-filtered automatically.*

## Step-by-step

### 1. Install the `[graph]` extra

`from_nodes` walks the network through a scipy sparse-graph index (`netstead.graph.GMNSGraph`); scipy ships in the `[graph]` extra. Without it the first scope call raises `ImportError: netstead.graph requires the [graph] extra: pip install 'netstead[graph]'`:

```bash
pip install 'netstead[graph]'
```

### 2. Decide `path_between=True` vs `False`

* `path_between=True` (default) — runs BFS shortest paths between every pair of seed nodes and includes all nodes + links on those paths. Gives you the *connected subgraph* containing the seeds.
* `path_between=False` — keeps just the seed nodes and their incident links. Useful when the seeds already describe a closed region and you don't want extra interior links.

### 3. Build the scope (lazy)

A `NetworkScope` is a description of *which rows* belong to the subset, not the subset itself. `scope.provenance` records how it was built (operation, seeds, parameters) for audit / debugging:

```python
import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
scope = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True)

print(f"nodes in scope:    {len(scope.node_ids)}")
print(f"links in scope:    {len(scope.link_ids)}")
print(f"provenance:        {scope.provenance}")   # str describing the op
```

### 4. Apply to materialize a sub-network

`.apply()` returns a normal `Network` you can validate, run quality checks on, or write out. Every table is pre-filtered by FK chain — lane rows whose `link_id` isn't in scope are dropped, signal rows for missing controllers are dropped, etc. A table the scope empties entirely (e.g. `signal_controller` when no signals fall in the subgraph) survives as a zero-row table with its schema intact:

```python
import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
scope = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True)

# Every table is FK-filtered to the scope:
#   link / node    — only ids in scope.link_ids / scope.node_ids
#   lane, link_tod — only rows whose link_id is in scope
#   geometry       — only ids referenced by surviving links
sub = scope.apply()
print(f"{sub.links.count()} links, {sub.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

### 5. Chain with set ops + buffers

Scopes compose with union / intersect / subtract and with network / spatial buffering. Build a corridor scope, union it with a second scope, then add a 100 m network buffer — all in one expression:

```python
import netstead
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.scope import from_nodes

net = netstead.read(leavenworth.csv_dir())
corridor = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50])
downtown = from_nodes(net, [10, 11, 12])

combined = corridor.union(downtown).buffer_network("100m")
# .intersect(other) and .subtract(other) compose the same way.
# .buffer_spatial(distance) buffers by straight-line distance in the geometry
# column's CRS units; it needs an inline link.geometry column and is a silent
# no-op on Leavenworth, which has none.
sub = combined.apply()
print(f"combined scope: {sub.links.count()} links, {sub.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

Expected:

```text
combined scope: 58 links, 24 nodes
```

### 6. CLI equivalent

The same operation runs from the shell. Add `--json` to any `netstead` (or `corral`) CLI command and the output becomes a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout — pipe into `jq`, save to a file, feed to a script or AI agent. Default output is human-readable rich panels:

```bash
netstead scope from-nodes packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv 1 25 50 --json
```

Expected:

```json
{
  "node_count": 14,
  "link_count": 28,
  "node_ids": [1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 15, 25, 50, 63, 74, 78, 96, 99, 100],
  "link_ids": [1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 27, 29, 30, 31, 34, 44, 46, 77, 79, 160, 196, 197, 225, 226, 238, 239, 283, 284, 290, 292, 293, 295],
  "provenance": "from_nodes([1, 25, 50], path_between=True)"
}
```

Every id in `node_ids` and `link_ids` is a plain integer.

## Common variations

???+ note "Default — multi-node BFS with path_between"
    Most common pattern: a handful of seed ids, paths between them filled in automatically.

    ```python
    sub = from_nodes(net, [1, 25, 50], path_between=True).apply()
    ```
