`ignore_missing` says what network_wrangler does when a selected record is not in the network: fail (`false`) or
skip it (`true`).

- **Picked links** are written by id with `ignore_missing: false`. A fix aimed at specific links should fail loudly
  when one of them is gone.
- **A query selection** keeps the query's own `ignore_missing`, which is `true` (network_wrangler's default) when
  the query has none. The plugin applies it now too: a resolved id the network no longer has is skipped and listed,
  instead of refusing the change.
- **Deletions** are written by id (the links the selection resolved to). Picked links get `ignore_missing: false`;
  links a query selected keep the query's flag, so with `true` a resolved link that is gone is skipped and listed,
  as for a property change. A deletion's nodes always get `false`.
- **Reading a card**, a selector without `ignore_missing` reads as `true`. A deletion keeps its links' flag; its
  nodes' flag is dropped and written back as `false`. The offline edit log's ids read as `false`.

## From Python

Each step is a recorded Action in the session history, so **Copy as Python** in the history strip replays it. The
copied lines import from `netstead_project_cards.actions`:

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| `project_cards.add_change` (`AddChange`) | Apply one change and add it to the network's draft. |
| `project_cards.undo_change` (`UndoChange`) | Undo the draft's last change. |
| `project_cards.remove_change` (`RemoveChange`) | Remove any change of the draft (the later ones are re-applied). |
| `project_cards.preview` (`PreviewChange`) | Preview a change on a copy of the network. |
| `project_cards.close_preview` (`ClosePreview`) | Close the preview. |
| `project_cards.commit` (`CommitCard`) | Write the draft as a card file and start a new draft. |
| `project_cards.import` (`ImportCard`) | Apply a card or edit log to the draft, all or nothing. |
| `project_cards.edit_card` (`EditCard`) | Load a catalog card into the draft to edit it, remembering its file. |
| `project_cards.open_catalog` (`OpenCatalog`) | Open a folder of card files as the catalog. |
| `project_cards.refresh_catalog` (`RefreshCatalog`) | Rescan the open catalog's folder. |
| `project_cards.check_card` (`CheckCard`) | Check whether a catalog card applies to the network now, without changing anything. |
| `project_cards.preview_card` (`PreviewCard`) | Preview a catalog card's changes on a copy of the network. |
| `project_cards.apply_card` (`ApplyCard`) | Apply a catalog card to the network, all or nothing; record it as applied. |
| `project_cards.rename_card` (`RenameCard`) | Rename a catalog card's file. |
| `project_cards.duplicate_card` (`DuplicateCard`) | Copy a catalog card to `<name>-copy.yml` (or a name you give). |
| `project_cards.delete_card` (`DeleteCard`) | Move a catalog card's file to the catalog's `.trash` folder. |
| `project_cards.restore_card` (`RestoreCard`) | Move a deleted card back from `.trash`. |
| `project_cards.update_card_meta` (`UpdateCardMeta`) | Change a catalog card's project, tags and dependencies. |
| `project_cards.session_summary` (`SessionSummary`) | The session summary as plain text. |

`session.dispatch` (or its alias `app.do`) runs them. A change targets the shared selection (`use_selection=True`),
a saved selection (`saved_selection="<name>"`, Python and the assistant only), or names its own facility. This
example opens the Leavenworth fixture, sets link 1 to two lanes, undoes a second change and commits the card to a
temporary folder. `plugins=[plugin()]` installs just this plugin; a `Session()` without it loads every installed
plugin, as `netstead app` does:

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.workbench import OpenNetwork, Select, Session
from netstead_project_cards import plugin
from netstead_project_cards.actions import AddChange, CommitCard, UndoChange
from netstead_project_cards.types import PropertyChange, RoadwayPropertyChange

fixture, out = leavenworth.parquet_dir(), Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
roots = {"io.allowed_roots": [str(out), str(fixture.parent)]}
app = Session(project_dir=out, overrides=roots, plugins=[plugin()])
app.dispatch(OpenNetwork(source=str(fixture)))
app.dispatch(Select(link_ids=[1]))
lanes = RoadwayPropertyChange(property_changes={"lanes": PropertyChange(existing=1, set=2)}, note="issue 42")
app.dispatch(AddChange(use_selection=True, change=lanes))
app.dispatch(AddChange(use_selection=True, change={"type": "roadway_property_change",
                                                   "property_changes": {"free_speed": {"change": -5}}}))
app.dispatch(UndoChange())  # takes back the free_speed change
result = app.dispatch(CommitCard(path=str(out / "link-1-lanes.yml"), project="Link 1 lanes", confirm_warnings=True))
print(result["card_id"], result["changes"])  # link-1-lanes 1
```

A change can be a model, as for `lanes`, or a plain dict, as in the copied lines. `confirm_warnings=True` stands in
for the dialog's confirmation: without it, a network with live edit warnings refuses the commit. The written file
loads with `projectcard`'s own reader:

```python
import projectcard

print(projectcard.read_card(out / "link-1-lanes.yml", validate=True).project)  # Link 1 lanes
```

Selecting by a request needs a language model (see [Explore in the Workbench](workbench.md)). Preview and import
work the same way:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead_project_cards.actions import ClosePreview, ImportCard, PreviewChange

app.dispatch(Select(utterance="Benton Street"))
app.dispatch(PreviewChange(use_selection=True, change={"type": "roadway_deletion"}))
app.dispatch(ClosePreview())
app.dispatch(ImportCard(path="cards/edit-log.yaml"))
```

Over HTTP, `POST /api/actions` takes the same Actions as JSON (`{"type": "project_cards.add_change", ...}`). The
panel also reads routes: `GET /api/plugins/project_cards/form` (the form for a change type on the selection),
`GET /api/plugins/project_cards/commit-check` (the warnings, problems and YAML the commit dialog shows), `/catalog`
(the open catalog), `/card` (the Inspect view) and `/summary.txt`. All only read.

The library behind the Actions is usable on its own: `DraftCard` builds a card from the change model and writes it
with `to_yaml()`, `read_card_file` reads one back, and `netstead_project_cards.validate.card_problems` runs
`projectcard`'s validator.

## With the assistant

The assistant offers a plugin's Actions only when you opt in. In **Settings → Assistant: actions & plugins**, or in
`~/.config/netstead/config.toml`:

```toml
[assistant]
plugins = ["project_cards"]
```

`plugins` is the opt-in. With a model on this machine (Ollama), the default `compact_tools = "auto"` gives it a smaller
set of tools. That set includes adding, undoing and previewing a change and closing the preview, but not committing
or importing, which need a file path. To draft those with a local model as well, set `compact_tools = "off"`.

Every `project_cards` Action changes a network, opens or closes a preview, or writes a file, so the assistant
drafts each one for you to approve. Nothing runs until you do. A drafted change made while a preview was open is
refused as stale if the previewed network has changed since.

## Pitfalls

- **Roadway only.** Transit change types answer "not yet supported" in the palette, the Actions and the
  assistant. `roadway_managed_lanes` and `pycode` are not supported either.
- **One number or text per property.** A card can't set a property to empty (clear a cell with a core edit
  instead) or to a list. `true` / `false` are written as `1` / `0`. Scoped (time-of-day) values are not supported.
- **A change must be a valid ProjectCard before it is applied.** For example, a request that names both a street and
  a route number gives a query that ProjectCard doesn't allow, so **Add to card** refuses it: select by one of them.
- **An added record's fields must be columns the network has.** A field with no column answers "not yet
  supported".
- **A draft lives in the Workbench session.** Closing the network or the app drops its draft. The network's edits
  stay pending until you save or discard them. Commit to keep the card.
- **A change that applies nothing is refused**, for example a query whose links are all gone with
  `ignore_missing: true`, or every property skipped by `skip`.
- **Importing a query needs provenance.** See [Import a card](#import-a-card).
- **The panel works on the shared selection.** To use a saved selection, select it first, or use
  `saved_selection` from Python or the assistant.
- **A committed card's id is not written to the network's lineage.** It is listed in the plugin's state
  (`plugins.project_cards.committed`) for the session.

## See also

- [Explore in the Workbench](workbench.md): selection, edits, the Edit tab, saving.
- [Write a Workbench plugin](workbench-plugins.md): the plugin API this plugin is built on.
- [Triage and fix findings](fix-findings.md): the offline report's edit log.
- [projectcard](https://github.com/network-wrangler/projectcard): the ProjectCard schema and validator.


<!-- source: cookbook/local-llm-ollama.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/local-llm-ollama.md -->

---
title: Run language models locally with Ollama
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Install Ollama, pull a small Qwen model, and use it for natural-language selection in the Workbench and the CLI. Nothing leaves your machine and there is no API key.
---

# Run language models locally with Ollama

## When to use this

You want natural-language selection ("I-40 EB between South Miami Boulevard and Airport
Boulevard") without sending anything to a cloud provider and without an API key. Ollama runs
open models such as Qwen on your own computer, and netstead talks to it over
`http://localhost:11434`.

## Why local

- **Nothing leaves your machine.** Your utterances, street names and project notes go to a
  server on `localhost`, not to a vendor.
- **Better answers by default — in the Workbench.** Because nothing leaves the machine, the
  `"auto"` quality settings turn on for a local endpoint there: grounding (the network's street
  names and route numbers), project notes (`NETSTEAD.md`) and the close-match retry. See
  [What is sent, and quality settings](workbench.md#what-is-sent-and-quality-settings). The CLI's
  `netstead select` sends only your utterance to the parser, with none of that extra context,
  whichever provider you choose.
- **No API key.** There is nothing to store or rotate.

The trade-off is that a small local model is slower than a hosted one on most laptops, and makes
more mistakes. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

## Install Ollama

Use the installer for your system from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). The
commands below come from Ollama's own download page and docs; if they have moved on, follow
ollama.com instead.

=== "macOS"

    Download the app from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download), open the `.dmg` and
    drag **Ollama** into **Applications**. Ollama's docs list macOS 14 Sonoma or newer. When the app
    first starts, it offers to put the `ollama` command on your `PATH`.

    Ollama's download page also offers the same install script as Linux. A Homebrew formula
    exists too, but it is community-maintained and isn't covered by Ollama's docs; the app is the
    supported route.

=== "Linux"

    Ollama's install script:

    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
    ```

    Piping a script into `sh` runs it with your permissions. Download it and read it first if you
    prefer:

    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh -o ollama-install.sh
    less ollama-install.sh
    sh ollama-install.sh
    ```

    Ollama's [Linux docs](https://docs.ollama.com/linux) also describe a manual install from a
    tarball.

=== "Windows"

    Download and run **OllamaSetup.exe** from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download).
    It installs for your account without administrator rights. Ollama's docs list Windows 10 22H2
    or newer. The download page also shows a PowerShell one-liner.

## Start it, then check it

- **macOS and Windows:** open the Ollama app. It runs the server in the background (on Windows,
  from the system tray).
- **Linux:** the install script normally sets Ollama up as a service. If it isn't running, start it
  with `sudo systemctl start ollama`, or run `ollama serve` in a terminal and leave it open.

By default the server listens on `127.0.0.1` port `11434`, which is also netstead's default
`llm.ollama.base_url`. Then check each layer:

```bash
ollama list                    # Ollama answers, and shows the models you have (none yet is fine)
uv run netstead llm status       # netstead can reach it; prints the next step if it can't
uv run netstead llm test ollama  # a token-free connection test
```

If Ollama is reachable but has no models, `netstead llm status` says
`next step: run: netstead llm pull qwen3:4b`. Once it has a model, the Ollama line names the model
selections will use, e.g. `running, 1 model(s); selections use qwen2.5:7b (qwen3:4b is not installed)`,
and `netstead llm test ollama` says the same.

## Get a model

**Already have a model?** You may not need to download anything. When you haven't chosen a model
and the default (`qwen3:4b`) isn't installed, netstead uses an installed one instead: the first
model from the table below that you have (in table order), else the first installed model that
Ollama reports as supporting tools. For example, if you only have `qwen2.5:7b`, the Workbench
and `netstead select --provider ollama` use it as is. A model you chose yourself (`--model`,
`select.model`, or the picker) is never replaced. If no installed model supports tools, netstead
asks you to pull the default.

Otherwise, pull the default, Qwen 3 4B (`qwen3:4b`). Any one of these does the same thing:

- In a terminal, with Ollama's own command:

    ```bash
    ollama pull qwen3:4b
    ```

- In a terminal, through netstead. It shows the size and asks before downloading (`--yes` skips
  the question), then shows a progress bar:

    ```bash
    uv run netstead llm pull qwen3:4b
    ```

- In the Workbench: open **Models…**. On the Ollama row, choose a model and click
  **Pull qwen3:4b**. Progress shows in the **Jobs** panel, where you can cancel it. When the pull
  finishes, the model appears in the picker. With models already installed, use
  **Pull another model**.

| Model | Download | When to choose it |
|---|---|---|
| `qwen3:4b` (default) | about 2.5 GB | Most laptops. Enough for one selection at a time. |
| `qwen3:8b` | about 5.2 GB | When `qwen3:4b` keeps misreading your phrases, and you have the memory to spare. Slower. |
| `qwen2.5:7b` | about 4.7 GB | If you already have it installed, it works: no need to pull another model. |

Sizes are the download sizes listed on [ollama.com/library/qwen3](https://ollama.com/library/qwen3)
and [ollama.com/library/qwen2.5](https://ollama.com/library/qwen2.5) (checked 2026-10-05). Both
library pages mark the models as supporting tools, which netstead uses.
Ollama doesn't publish memory requirements per model. As a rough guide, you need at least the
download size free in memory, plus some overhead, to run a model comfortably. netstead asks for a
16,384-token context window (`llm.ollama.num_ctx`), about 0.7 GB more than Ollama's default for `qwen2.5:7b`, which takes
5.0 GB loaded. If your machine starts swapping, use the smaller model, or lower `num_ctx` to 8192 (the
assistant's prompt may then be cut off).

The Workbench only pulls into an Ollama on this machine, and only when the Workbench itself is
bound to this machine (the default, `127.0.0.1`). Otherwise, pull from a terminal.

## Use it in the Workbench

1. Start the Workbench: `uv run netstead app ./my-network`.
2. Choose **Ollama (local)** in the provider picker next to the utterance box, then pick a model.
   The picker lists the models Ollama has installed, and starts on the model selections will use.
   If that isn't the default because the default isn't installed, hovering over the model says so.
3. That choice applies to this session. Click **Make default** to save it to your user config.

Common requests ("Cedar St between Central Ave and Price Ave", "all residential links") are answered by the
offline pattern parser without calling the model; the model is called for the rest. A local 7B model takes a few
seconds per call on a laptop, plus the time to load it into memory on the first call
([timings](find-links.md#performance)). netstead asks Ollama to keep the model loaded for 30 minutes after each
call (`llm.ollama.keep_alive`; Ollama's own default is 5), so the load comes only after a longer pause.

Or set it in a config file:

```toml
# ~/.config/netstead/config.toml (or ./netstead.toml for one project)
[select]
provider = "ollama"
model = "qwen3:4b"
```

From a terminal:

```bash
uv run netstead select "I-40 EB between South Miami Boulevard and Airport Boulevard" ./my-network --provider ollama --model qwen3:4b
```

Without `--model` (and with no `select.model` set), `netstead select` uses the model
`netstead llm status` names.

## Ollama on another machine

A GPU workstation on your network can run the model for everyone. Point netstead at it, either in
**Models… → Ollama server** or in the config file:

```toml
[llm.ollama]
base_url = "http://gpu-box.example:11434"
```

An address that isn't this machine counts as **remote**: your utterances now leave your computer.
So the `"auto"` quality settings turn **off**, the same as for a cloud provider, and the
Workbench won't pull models there (run `ollama pull` on that server). If you trust that
server with your network's street names and project notes, opt back in:

```toml
[llm.quality]
grounding = "on"        # send street names and route numbers
project_context = "on"  # send NETSTEAD.md / the ## netstead section
match_retry = "on"      # after a miss, retry with the closest real names
```

Ollama only listens on `127.0.0.1` unless it is told otherwise. Ollama's
[FAQ](https://docs.ollama.com/faq) explains how to expose it with `OLLAMA_HOST`.

## Troubleshooting

**"could not reach Ollama at http://localhost:11434" / connection refused.** Ollama isn't running,
or isn't installed. Open the app (macOS/Windows), or run `ollama serve` (Linux), then
`uv run netstead llm test ollama`. In the Workbench, click **Check again**. If you changed
`llm.ollama.base_url`, check the address and port.

**"model not found" / the model shows "(not installed)".** Pull it: `ollama pull qwen3:4b`,
`uv run netstead llm pull qwen3:4b`, or **Pull** in the Workbench. Model names must match what
`ollama list` prints, including the tag after the colon.

**Slow answers.** Without a supported GPU, Ollama runs on the CPU, and each selection can take
many seconds. `ollama ps` shows whether a loaded model is on the GPU or CPU. Use `qwen3:4b` rather
than a larger model. If requests time out, raise `llm.ollama.timeout_s` (default 120 seconds). The
assistant's prompt is about 5,000 tokens, so an **Ask** waits longer than a **Find** before the model
starts answering: 5–30 s per call for `qwen2.5:7b` on an M3 laptop.

**A model without tool support.** netstead asks for a tool call first. If Ollama answers that the
model "does not support tools", netstead automatically retries the same model in JSON mode,
constrained to the same schema. You don't need to do anything.

**More misreadings than a hosted model.** Small models make more mistakes. Try, in order:

1. Keep `llm.quality.temperature` at its default, `0`. In our tests `qwen2.5:7b` read every one of
   a set of varied requests correctly at temperature 0, and misread a few street names as route
   numbers at Ollama's own default temperature. When that happens and the "route number" matches
   no route in your network, netstead looks it up as a street name instead, and the selection's
   diagnostics say so (`treated ref 'Capital Blvd' as a street name`). It does the same for a
   route number read as a street name. A value that does match its own column is used as is.
2. Give the model another attempt after an invalid reply:

    ```toml
    [llm.quality]
    max_repairs = 2
    ```

3. Switch to `qwen3:8b`.
4. Add a `NETSTEAD.md` with your local names ("the Beltline" is I 440). See
   [Project notes](workbench.md#project-notes).

## See also

- [Find links by describing them](find-links.md) — what to type, which requests skip the model entirely, and
  timings with `qwen2.5:7b`.
- [Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench](workbench.md#language-models-natural-language-selection) — every provider, keys, quality settings.
- [Ollama documentation](https://docs.ollama.com) — install, the CLI, and the API.


<!-- source: cookbook/view-your-network.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/view-your-network.md -->

---
title: View a network on a map (with or without findings)
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Render a self-contained interactive Leaflet map of any GMNS network — useful for sanity-checks, demos, and bug reports. The same renderer is what `netstead validate --html` wraps; here you use it directly, with or without validation overlays.
---

# View a network on a map

## When to use this

You want a one-file, send-it-to-a-colleague visual of a GMNS network — without
having to spin up a Jupyter notebook, a geopandas plot, or a folium map. Maybe
to confirm an OSM build covered the right area, demo the result of an edit,
attach to a bug report, or check that quality-rule findings cluster where you
expect them.

The renderer is the same one `netstead validate --html` uses. Calling it
directly lets you pass any list of [`Issue`][issue] objects (validation,
quality, graph topology, custom) as overlays — or none at all.

## Quick example

Render the bundled Leavenworth fixture to a single HTML file. The renderer lives in `netstead.map`; nothing is overlaid because no issues are passed:

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth
from netstead.map import render_network_html

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
open("net.html", "w").write(render_network_html(net, title="Leavenworth"))
```

Open `net.html` in any browser. You'll see the link geometry as a thin
underlay on a Leaflet base map. No overlay markers because no issues were
passed.

## Step-by-step

### 1. Overlay validation findings

`render_validation_html` takes the network and a `ValidationReport` and composes the map with the findings table — it is what `netstead validate --html` writes:

```python
from netstead.map import render_validation_html

report = net.validate()
open("net.html", "w").write(render_validation_html(net, report))
```

Each finding becomes a clickable marker, color-coded by severity. A **Resources** table above the findings
lists every spec resource (required/optional, present, row count). Cross-cutting findings (no row, no coords)
sit in a collapsed "Unlocated findings" `<details>` block, with its count in the summary — still clickable for
the row-sync when expanded. Findings that share a code and differ only by resource (such as the sixteen
`structural.missing_optional_resource` lines a partial GMNS package produces) are grouped into one line there.

### 2. Overlay anything else

The renderer accepts a flat `list[Issue]`, so any `Issue` source plugs in
without renderer changes:

```python
from corral.reports import Category, Issue, Severity

custom = [
    Issue(
        severity=Severity.WARNING,
        category=Category.DATA_QUALITY,
        code="quality.signage_missing",
        message="no stop sign at intersection 42",
        extra={"lon": -120.66, "lat": 47.59},
    ),
]
open("net.html", "w").write(render_network_html(net, custom))
```

GMNS-specific data-quality rules (`netstead.quality.*`) already produce
`Issue` objects in this shape, so `run_quality(net).issues` drops straight in.

### 3. OpenStreetMap deep links

When the network has `osm_way_id` (and optionally `osm_node_id`) columns —
as produced by `netstead build`, the OSM importer — each marker's popup
carries an "Edit in OSM" link straight to the iD editor at
`openstreetmap.org/edit?editor=id&way=<id>`. Pass `osm_editor="josm"` to
target the desktop JOSM editor instead (via its localhost
RemoteControl plugin).

## Common variations

??? note "Different base map"
    ```python
    render_network_html(net, tile_provider="openstreetmap")  # default is "esri", a keyless light grey
    ```

??? note "Embed in a Jupyter notebook"
    ```python
    from IPython.display import IFrame
    open("/tmp/net.html", "w").write(render_network_html(net, report.issues))
    IFrame("/tmp/net.html", 900, 600)
    ```

??? note "From the CLI"
    `netstead validate --html` writes this same page with the findings overlaid:

    ```bash
    netstead validate <source> --html report.html  # findings overlay
    ```

    For *interactive* viewing — linked map and table, validation, editing —
    open the network in the Workbench instead; this renderer is for a
    self-contained, offline HTML file you can send to someone:

    ```bash
    netstead app <source>
    ```

    See [Explore in the Workbench](workbench.md).

## Pitfalls

* **Requires the `[reports]` extra.** `pip install 'netstead[reports]'`
  (pulls in `jinja2`, `openpyxl` and `pyyaml`). Leaflet itself is vendored —
  no internet required when the report is opened.
* **No marker clustering yet.** Past a few thousand findings the Leaflet
  canvas slows down. Filter the issue list before passing it in.
* **`title=` controls the `<title>` tag.** It does not override how the
  network's spec version / link / node counts appear in the subtitle.

## See also

* [Validate a network](validate-network.md) — `--html` / `--csv` / `--xlsx`
  CLI flags wrap the same renderer.
* [Build from OSM](build-from-osm.md) — produces a network with
  `osm_way_id` columns so the "Edit in OSM" links light up.
* [Customize quality](customize-quality.md) — quality rules feed the same
  `Issue` overlay path.

[issue]: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/api/reports/#corral.reports.Issue


<!-- source: cookbook/serve-http.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/serve-http.md -->

---
title: Self-host the HTTP server
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Run the FastAPI server with bearer-token auth, configure packages, and stand it up behind a reverse proxy.
---

# Self-host the HTTP server

## When to use this

You want HTTP access to your GMNS networks — for dashboards, non-Python consumers, or a small team sharing a single curated set of packages. The server is read-only: it serves metadata, the resolved spec, validation reports and quality reports, never edits.

## Quick example

Write a minimal config that binds localhost on port 8000, requires a bearer token, and exposes one package. Start it with `netstead server run`:

```yaml
# server.yaml
bind: 127.0.0.1
port: 8000
auth:
  kind: bearer
  token: "paste-the-output-of-generate_dev_token-here"
packages:
  - id: leavenworth
    source: packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
```

```bash
netstead server run --config server.yaml
```

Expected:

```text
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

![Interactive OpenAPI docs for the netstead HTTP server](../assets/screenshots/serve-http-openapi.png){ .screenshot }
*Interactive OpenAPI at `/docs` — every endpoint with try-it-out forms and the JSON response schema.*

## Step-by-step

### 1. Install the `[server]` extra

`[server]` brings in FastAPI, uvicorn and pydantic-settings. Add `[graph]` as well if you want `/networks/{id}/quality` — the GMNS rule pack's connectivity rule needs scipy:

```bash
pip install 'netstead[server,graph]'
```

### 2. Generate a dev token

`generate_dev_token()` returns one URL-safe random string (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`). The same string goes into the config and into every client's `Authorization` header — the server stores it as given, it does not hash it:

```bash
python -c "from corral.api import generate_dev_token; print(generate_dev_token())"
```

Expected (yours will differ):

```text
D--IvW8W34gDhwRQC2D9ro9mhSEfPXsPX8XnBV8UUaU
```

Paste it into `auth.token` in your config and keep it with the same care as any other shared secret.

### 3. Write a config YAML

A config is one `ServerSettings` document (`corral.api.config`): `bind`, `port`, an `auth` block and a `packages` list. Each package has a URL-safe `id`, a `source` that `Network.from_source` accepts, and an optional `description` echoed by `/networks`. There are no per-package engine or spec-version keys and no logging section — the spec version is detected from the data, and logging is uvicorn's:

```yaml
# server.yaml
bind: 127.0.0.1      # 0.0.0.0 to accept off-host requests (see pitfalls)
port: 8000

auth:
  kind: bearer       # or "none" — see pitfalls
  token: "paste-the-output-of-generate_dev_token-here"

packages:
  - id: leavenworth
    source: packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
    description: Bundled Leavenworth, WA fixture (GMNS 0.97)
  - id: regional
    source: s3://my-bucket/regional/datapackage.json
```

JSON works too (`--config server.json`). YAML parsing uses `pyyaml`, which `uvicorn[standard]` (part of the `[server]` extra) already installs.

### 4. Run it + verify

Start the server, then hit `/health` (the unauthenticated liveness probe) to confirm it's up. `--bind` / `--port` override the config for a one-off run:

```bash
netstead server run --config server.yaml
```

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
```

Expected:

```json
{"status": "ok"}
```

### 5. Make authenticated requests

Pass the token from step 2 as a bearer header. Every response is JSON, whatever `Accept` header the client sends. `/networks` is the cheap listing — it echoes the config without loading anything:

```bash
TOKEN="paste-the-output-of-generate_dev_token-here"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8000/networks
```

Expected:

```json
[{"id": "leavenworth", "source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv", "description": "Bundled Leavenworth, WA fixture (GMNS 0.97)"}]
```

Counts and the spec version are on the per-network endpoint, which loads the package on first access:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8000/networks/leavenworth
```

Expected:

```json
{"id": "leavenworth", "name": "gmns", "spec_version": "0.97", "engine": "IbisEngine", "links": 339, "nodes": 121, "table_count": 9, "tables": ["geometry", "lane", "link", "link_tod", "node", "signal_controller", "time_set_definitions", "use_definition", "use_group"]}
```

Quality checks are a `POST` (a `GET` returns `405 Method Not Allowed`). The body is the same `ValidationReport.to_dict()` shape the CLI's `--json` emits:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     http://127.0.0.1:8000/networks/leavenworth/quality
```

### 6. Endpoint list

| Endpoint | Returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `{"status": "ok"}` (no auth) |
| `GET /packages` | `[{id, source, description}]` — configured packages, nothing loaded |
| `GET /packages/{id}` | `{id, name, engine, table_count, tables: [{name, rows, columns}]}` |
| `GET /packages/{id}/spec` | resolved Frictionless `datapackage.json` |
| `POST /packages/{id}/validate` | full validation report (`ValidationReport.to_dict()`); packages are loaded as `Network`s, so this is GMNS validation with `spec_version` set |
| `GET /networks` | same listing as `/packages` |
| `GET /networks/{id}` | `{id, name, spec_version, engine, links, nodes, table_count, tables}` |
| `POST /networks/{id}/quality` | the GMNS rule pack as a validation report (needs `[graph]`) |

Interactive OpenAPI at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`.

## Common variations

???+ note "Default — localhost bind with bearer auth"
    Safe default for dev and single-host production behind a reverse proxy.

    ```yaml
    bind: 127.0.0.1
    auth: { kind: bearer, token: "..." }
    ```

??? note "Off-host access (LAN, etc.)"
    Bind `0.0.0.0` — but keep auth on.

    ```yaml
    bind: 0.0.0.0
    auth: { kind: bearer, token: "..." }
    ```

??? note "Behind nginx / Caddy"
    Bind to `127.0.0.1`; let the proxy terminate TLS and forward. No server-side TLS config needed.

    ```yaml
    bind: 127.0.0.1
    port: 8000
    ```

??? note "One token per client"
    The config holds exactly one `auth.token`. To give each client its own credential, run one server process (and config) per client, or put an authenticating reverse proxy in front and let it hold the per-client secrets.

??? note "Disable auth (dev only)"
    The server still starts on a public bind with `kind: none` — it only logs a warning (see pitfalls) — so pair this with a localhost bind.

    ```yaml
    bind: 127.0.0.1
    auth: { kind: none }
    ```

??? note "Docker"
    The repo ships a server image definition at `packages/netstead/Dockerfile` (plus `docker-compose.example.yml` beside it). Build it from the repo root — the build needs both workspace packages — and mount your config and data:

    ```bash
    docker build -f packages/netstead/Dockerfile -t netstead-server .
    docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
        -v $(pwd)/server.yaml:/etc/netstead/config.yml:ro \
        -v $(pwd)/data:/data:ro \
        netstead-server
    ```

    A prebuilt `ghcr.io` image is not published yet (tracked in [#104](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/issues/104)). Alternatively, `pip install` into your own image and copy the config alongside:

    ```dockerfile
    FROM python:3.12-slim
    RUN pip install 'netstead[server,graph]'
    COPY server.yaml /etc/netstead/server.yaml
    CMD ["netstead", "server", "run", "--config", "/etc/netstead/server.yaml"]
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **`auth.kind: none` + non-localhost bind is a security footgun.** The server logs a `corral.api: auth.kind='none' with bind='0.0.0.0' exposes the server with NO authentication` warning at startup and then runs anyway — there is no refuse-to-start guard and no override key. Treat the warning as a stop sign.
* **Bearer mode needs a token.** `kind: bearer` without `auth.token` fails at app build time (`AuthSettings(kind='bearer') requires token to be set`), so a misconfigured server never silently lets requests through.
* **Tokens are compared in constant time, as plaintext.** The server holds the token string from the config and checks the incoming `Authorization: Bearer …` header against it with `hmac.compare_digest`. There is no hashing — protect the config file as you would the token itself.
* **Packages are cached after first load.** The `PackageRegistry` loads each package through `Network.from_source` the first time its id is requested and keeps it for the life of the process. Edit the files on disk, or the config, and you need to restart the server to see the change.
* **No write endpoints.** The HTTP server is read-only by design. For editing, use the Python API + `Session`, or the Workbench.

## See also

* [Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop](serve-mcp.md) — same data, stdio transport.
* [MCP tools reference](../ai/mcp-tools.md) — what the MCP surface exposes.
* [corral API reference](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/reference/api/) — `corral.api.ServerSettings`, `AuthSettings`, `PackageRef`, `generate_dev_token`, `load_settings`.


<!-- source: cookbook/serve-mcp.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/serve-mcp.md -->

---
title: Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Run netstead as an MCP server over stdio so an AI agent can call its tools — install, configure, list of bundled tools, sample prompts.
---

# Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop

## When to use this

You want an AI agent (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, any MCP-aware host) to call `netstead` directly via tool calls — describe a package, run validation, scope a subgraph, run the quality pack — instead of you copying CLI output into the chat. The MCP server speaks the Model Context Protocol so the agent treats `netstead` as a first-class tool surface.

## Quick example

Add this entry to your MCP host config, restart the host, and ask the agent "describe the package at /tmp/leavenworth/csv". The agent picks `describe_package`, calls it with `{"source": "/tmp/leavenworth/csv"}`, and surfaces the package name, engine, table count and each table's row count and columns back in chat:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netstead": {
      "command": "netstead",
      "args": ["mcp", "serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

Once connected, Claude lists the seven netstead tools and calls them with the `source` path you name; the tool name, its
arguments and the JSON reply appear inline in the chat.

## Step-by-step

### 1. Install

The `[mcp]` extra brings in `mcp` (the official Python SDK, v1 API). Add `[graph]` too: `connected_components` and `quality_check` need scipy, and without it those two tools fail at call time:

```bash
pip install 'netstead[mcp,graph]'
```

### 2. Test the server runs

You don't normally launch the server yourself — the MCP host does it. But `--help` confirms the entry point resolves and the SDK is importable:

```bash
netstead mcp serve --help
```

Expected:

```text
Usage: netstead mcp serve [OPTIONS]

 Start the netstead MCP server on stdio (for Claude Desktop / Claude Code).
 ...
╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --name          TEXT  MCP server display name. [default: netstead] │
│ --help  -h            Show this message and exit.                  │
╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### 3. Configure the MCP host

**Claude Desktop (macOS):** edit `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`. On Linux it's `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`; on Windows, `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`. Restart Claude Desktop after editing; the tools show up under a hammer-icon in the chat input:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netstead": {
      "command": "netstead",
      "args": ["mcp", "serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

**Claude Code:** register the server from the terminal — everything after `--` is the command Claude Code launches:

```bash
claude mcp add netstead -- netstead mcp serve
```

`--scope project` writes it to a `.mcp.json` at the project root that teammates pick up on session start (the default scope is local to you); see `claude mcp add --help`. The equivalent hand-written `.mcp.json` is the same JSON as above. To use the version installed in a project venv, replace `netstead` with the absolute path to that venv's `netstead`.

### 4. The tools shipped today

The server exposes seven stateless tools. Every tool takes a `source` — any path or URL that `Network.from_source` accepts — and returns JSON; only `scope_from_nodes` takes anything more. Full input and output shapes are in the [MCP tools reference](../ai/mcp-tools.md).

| Name | Summary | Inputs | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `describe_package` | Generic package overview: name, engine, table count, per-table rows + columns. | `source` | `{source, name, engine, table_count, tables: [{name, rows, columns}]}` |
| `validate_package` | Generic Frictionless validation (no GMNS spec). For GMNS use `netstead validate --json`. | `source` | `ValidationReport.to_dict()` |
| `list_tables` | Sorted table names, no row counts. | `source` | `["lane", "link", ...]` |
| `describe_network` | GMNS-aware overview: spec version, link + node counts, table names. | `source` | `{source, name, spec_version, engine, links, nodes, table_count, tables}` |
| `quality_check` | The GMNS data-quality rule pack. Needs `[graph]`. | `source` | `ValidationReport.to_dict()` |
| `connected_components` | Count + sizes of weakly-connected components. Needs `[graph]`. | `source` | `{source, component_count, sizes}` |
| `scope_from_nodes` | Node-seeded scope; returns the resulting node + link id sets. | `source`, `node_ids: [int]`, `path_between: bool = true` | `{source, seed_node_ids, path_between, result_node_count, result_link_count, node_ids, link_ids}` |

### 5. Sample agent prompts

Each of these exercises a different tool — paste them into a chat with the server configured to see the agent pick the right call:

* **"What's in the GMNS network at `packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv`?"** — agent calls `describe_network`, returns spec version `0.97`, 339 links, 121 nodes and the nine table names.
* **"Run the quality rules on that network and summarize the warnings by code."** — agent calls `quality_check`, groups the `issues` list by `code`, and reports the counts.
* **"Scope the network to the shortest paths between nodes 1, 25 and 50 and tell me how many links that is."** — agent calls `scope_from_nodes` with `node_ids=[1, 25, 50]` and `path_between=true` (the default). See the known issue on this tool in the [MCP tools reference](../ai/mcp-tools.md#scope_from_nodessource-node_ids-path_between).

## Common variations

???+ note "Default — stdio transport, system netstead"
    The simplest config: relies on `netstead` being on the MCP host's `PATH`.

    ```json
    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "netstead": { "command": "netstead", "args": ["mcp", "serve"] }
      }
    }
    ```

??? note "Rename the server in the host UI"
    `--name` becomes the label under the tool list in Claude.

    ```json
    "args": ["mcp", "serve", "--name", "gmns-leavenworth"]
    ```

??? note "Run inside a project venv"
    Use the absolute path to that venv's `netstead` binary; avoids version skew with the system install.

    ```json
    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "netstead": {
          "command": "/path/to/.venv/bin/netstead",
          "args": ["mcp", "serve"]
        }
      }
    }
    ```

??? note "Pin the server to a working directory"
    Adds `cwd` so all relative-path tool calls resolve from a known root.

    ```json
    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "netstead": {
          "command": "netstead",
          "args": ["mcp", "serve"],
          "cwd": "/abs/path/to/data"
        }
      }
    }
    ```

??? note "Pass env vars (cloud creds)"
    Use `env` to inject credentials into the subprocess.

    ```json
    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "netstead": {
          "command": "netstead",
          "args": ["mcp", "serve"],
          "env": { "AWS_PROFILE": "ds-readonly" }
        }
      }
    }
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **Stdio transport only today.** The HTTP MCP transport is a follow-up — track the [open issues](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/issues?q=mcp) for progress. For now, every agent that wants to call netstead needs to launch its own subprocess.
* **Tools are stateless.** There's no persistent `edit_session` tool yet — every call is a one-shot load + read. The agent can't mutate a network and inspect intermediate state across calls. See the [issue tracker](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/issues?q=mcp) for the design discussion.
* **JSON-only return values.** Tool outputs are summaries (counts, names, id lists, reports), never table rows. For the data itself, the agent should call the CLI or the Python API through a shell tool.
* **Config file path is case-sensitive on macOS.** `Claude` vs `claude` matters. If the server doesn't show up after a restart, check `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp*.log`.

## See also

* [Architecture](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/architecture/) — MCP server position in the v1.0 surface layering.
* [Drive the CLI from an AI agent loop](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/ai/json-cli/) — when you want an agent to drive `netstead` via shell instead of MCP.
* [API reference](../reference/api.md) — the Python entry points the MCP tools wrap.


<!-- source: cookbook/run-bench.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/cookbook/run-bench.md -->

---
title: Run the bundled benchmarks
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: netstead bench measures load + validate + connectivity timings per phase on your network + hardware.
---

# Run the bundled benchmarks

## When to use this

You want a fast read on how `netstead` performs on your hardware against your network — sizing a server, comparing hardware or storage formats, or tracking CI regressions over time.

## Quick example

Run the bench against the bundled Leavenworth fixture. Add `--json` to any `netstead` (or `corral`) CLI command and the output becomes a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout — pipe into `jq`, save to a file, feed to a script or AI agent. Default output is human-readable rich panels:

```bash
netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json
```

Expected:

```json
{
  "source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv",
  "engine": "IbisEngine",
  "total_seconds": "...",
  "phases": [
    {"phase": "load",         "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "validate",     "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "links_count",  "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "nodes_count",  "seconds": "..."},
    {"phase": "is_connected", "seconds": "..."}
  ]
}
```

The `"..."` values are timings in seconds (floats such as `0.112`); they vary by machine and run, so they're elided here.

## Step-by-step

### 1. Run against the bundled reference

The Leavenworth fixture is small (339 links / 121 nodes) — total runtime is under a second. It's a baseline, not a benchmark; useful for confirming nothing's wrong with the install:

```bash
netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
```

### 2. Run against your own network

Same command, different path. The bench accepts the same source surface as `Network.from_source` — local dirs, `s3://`, `duckdb://`, etc.:

```bash
netstead bench /path/to/my/network --json > bench.json
```

### 3. Compare storage formats

DuckDB (via ibis) is the single compute engine, so there is no engine to sweep — `--engine` is accepted only for compatibility. What *does* move the numbers is the on-disk format you load from. Convert the same network to CSV and Parquet and bench each:

```bash
netstead bench /path/to/net-csv --json > csv.json
netstead bench /path/to/net-parquet --json > parquet.json
```

### 4. Capture a baseline for CI

For regression tracking, save a baseline JSON in-repo and compare on every PR. A 30% tolerance is reasonable for the Leavenworth fixture given timing noise; tighten on larger networks:

```bash
netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json > bench-baseline.json
# in CI:
netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json > bench-current.json
python -c "
import json
b = json.load(open('bench-baseline.json'))['total_seconds']
c = json.load(open('bench-current.json'))['total_seconds']
assert c < b * 1.3, f'regression: {c:.2f}s vs baseline {b:.2f}s (+{(c/b-1)*100:.0f}%)'
"
```

### 5. Read the JSON

The shape is stable inside a major version. Each phase is one logical operation: `load` opens the package; `validate` runs the structural + schema passes only (`net.validate(foreign_keys=False, sync_state=False)` — no FK or sync-state checks); `links_count` / `nodes_count` force a count on each table; `is_connected` builds the scipy `GMNSGraph` and checks that there is a single weakly-connected component:

```json
{
  "source": "packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv",
  "engine": "IbisEngine",
  "total_seconds": 0.555,
  "phases": [
    {"phase": "load",         "seconds": 0.112},
    {"phase": "validate",     "seconds": 0.130},
    {"phase": "links_count",  "seconds": 0.002},
    {"phase": "nodes_count",  "seconds": 0.001},
    {"phase": "is_connected", "seconds": 0.309}
  ]
}
```

## Common variations

???+ note "Default — Leavenworth fixture, JSON out"
    Quickest smoke-test that the install works and the engine is wired up.

    ```bash
    netstead bench packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv --json
    ```

??? note "Just the total seconds (for shell pipelines)"
    Pipe through `jq` to extract a single number.

    ```bash
    netstead bench ./my-net --json | jq -r .total_seconds
    ```

??? note "Phase breakdown as CSV"
    For charting or copying into a spreadsheet.

    ```bash
    netstead bench ./my-net --json | jq -r '.phases[] | [.phase,.seconds] | @csv'
    ```

??? note "CI regression check (one-liner)"
    Fails the CI step if the total exceeds your budget.

    ```bash
    netstead bench ./my-net --json | jq -e '.total_seconds < 5.0'
    ```

??? note "Format sweep"
    Loop over copies of the same network in different storage formats.

    ```bash
    for d in ./my-net-csv ./my-net-parquet; do
      netstead bench "$d" --json > "bench-$(basename "$d").json"
    done
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **Micro-network timing is noisy.** On Leavenworth the absolute numbers fluctuate by ±30% between runs. Use it to confirm correctness, not for sizing decisions — switch to a regional-scale network before drawing conclusions.
* **Every CLI run is a cold start.** Each `netstead bench` invocation is a fresh process, so the `is_connected` phase always includes building the scipy `GMNSGraph` — there is no cache to warm by running the command twice. The graph is cached on the `Network` object only within one Python process (a second `is_connected(net)` call on the same object is faster).
* **Connectivity requires `[graph]`.** Without scipy the `is_connected` phase is skipped and reported as `{"phase": "is_connected", "seconds": null, "skipped": "scipy not installed"}`; `total_seconds` sums the phases that ran. Data-quality rules are not part of `netstead bench`.

## Run the benchmark suite (`netstead bench-suite`)

`netstead bench` times one network end to end. `netstead bench-suite` sweeps *size tiers* over three operation families — `network_create` (load the fixture from each committed storage format, with row counts asserted as a correctness check), `selection` (resolve the versioned natural-language selection cases through the stub parser, cold and warm) and `viz_pack` (pack the network into the browser payload, timing plus byte counts) — and emits one structured document with wall time and peak memory per case. It needs the `[bench]` extra (`psutil`, for process RSS); the `selection` family also wants `[nl]` and returns nothing without it, and live OSM builds want `[osm]`:

```bash
pip install 'netstead[bench]'
netstead bench-suite --sizes S,M --format md --output bench.md
```

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--sizes` | `S,M` | Size tiers to sweep, comma-separated from `S`, `M`, `L`. |
| `--operations` | `network_create,selection,viz_pack` | Operation families to run, comma-separated. |
| `--format` | `json` | `json` (the canonical regression document), `csv` (flattened results) or `md` (a table with an environment stamp). |
| `--output` / `-o` | stdout | Write the rendered document to this file. |
| `--repeats` | `3` | Macro timing repeats (reported as median + min). |
| `--warm-repeats` | `20` | Repeats for the warm selection number. |
| `--run-osm` | off | Include live OSM builds (hits Overpass). |
| `--fixtures` | `benchmarks/fixtures.toml` | Override the fixture registry file. |
| `--commit` | — | Git SHA to stamp into the environment block. |

Fixture definitions live in `benchmarks/fixtures.toml` at the repo root (a built-in default covering the bundled fixtures is used when the file isn't found). The `S` tier (Leavenworth, 339 links) and `M` tier (`rdu_i40`) ship inside the wheel. The `L` tier is never committed: point `NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE` at a GMNS package directory or a `.duckdb` file, or set `NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE_BBOX="west,south,east,north"` and pass `--run-osm` to build it live from OpenStreetMap:

```bash
export NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE=/path/to/large-network
netstead bench-suite --sizes S,M,L --format json --output bench.json
```

## Bench the OSM build path (`scripts/bench_osm_build.py`)

A separate harness measures the *construction* of a network from OpenStreetMap (convert + `Network` assembly on the DuckDB engine) and, optionally, compares it against `osmnx` and `osm2gmns` as directional baselines. It lives at `scripts/bench_osm_build.py`. Examples:

```bash
# Synthetic grids (no network I/O — reproducible, fast).
uv run python scripts/bench_osm_build.py --grids 10,40,100

# Real bbox (one Overpass fetch, reused by the netstead build + the osmnx baseline).
uv run python scripts/bench_osm_build.py --bbox=-120.6794,47.5751,-120.6411,47.6082 --baselines
```

Representative numbers (M1 / macOS; absolute numbers are noisy ±30%). The first dataset in a run also pays one-time import / DuckDB warm-up, so treat it as a cold-start figure:

| Dataset | tool | build | peak mem | result (nodes / links) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| grid 10×10 (100 nodes / 20 ways) | netstead | 0.17 s | 2.6 MB | 100 / 360 |
| grid 40×40 (1.6k nodes / 80 ways) | netstead | 0.05 s | 1.2 MB | 1600 / 6240 |
| grid 100×100 (10k nodes / 200 ways) | netstead | 0.08 s | 5.3 MB | 10000 / 39600 |
| Leavenworth bbox (8.5k OSM nodes → 1.9k GMNS nodes / 4.3k directed links) | netstead | 0.13 s | 2.6 MB | 1871 / 4250 |
| Leavenworth bbox (same area) | osmnx | 1.11 s | 20.3 MB | 1871 / ~4250 (directional) |

Takeaways:

* The **osmnx baseline** is intentionally directional, not apples-to-apples — `osmnx` performs its own simplification and uses a different directed-link convention. Use it as a sanity check that we're in the same order of magnitude, not as a strict speed comparison.
* The `osm2gmns` baseline needs a local `--osm-file` and a C/C++ toolchain to install; when it is missing, the harness prints the install command and skips that baseline cleanly.
* There is no engine axis: DuckDB (via ibis) is the single compute engine. For the broader create / selection / viz-pack timing suite, use `netstead bench-suite`.

## See also

* [Convert CSV ↔ Parquet ↔ DuckDB](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/cookbook/convert-formats/) — the format you load from dominates `load` time.
* [API reference](../reference/api.md) — `Network.from_source()` + `.validate()` for programmatic equivalents. The timing harness is also importable: `netstead.bench` exports the capture primitives (`time_call`, `memory_call`, `repeat_wall_seconds`, …) and report renderers (`build_document`, `render_json` / `render_csv` / `render_markdown`), and `netstead.bench.suite.run_suite(...)` runs the same suite as `netstead bench-suite`.

---
title: CLI reference
audience: both

summary: Every netstead command and sub-command with its arguments and options, generated from the CLI at build time.

# CLI reference

## Summary

`netstead` is the command-line front door to the library: inspect, validate, convert, build, scope,
clean and benchmark GMNS networks, and start the HTTP, MCP and Workbench servers. The command tree
below is generated from the live typer app (`netstead.cli.app`) on every docs build, so it cannot
drift from the installed version; `netstead --help` and `netstead <command> --help` print the same
text in the terminal.

Three conventions apply across the tree:

- **`--json`.** Every data command accepts `--json` and then writes exactly one JSON document to
  stdout, so the result pipes into `jq` or straight into an agent. The index table marks which
  commands take it.
- **`netstead doctor`** is an *install* doctor: Python version, optional extras, vendored spec
  versions, and whether the bundled Leavenworth fixture loads. To diagnose a network, use
  `netstead validate` (spec, schema and foreign-key checks) or `netstead quality` (data-quality rules).
- **Optional extras.** Commands that need an extra (`server`, `mcp`, `clean`, `osm`, `reports`, ...)
  are always listed in `--help`. When the extra is missing they exit with code 1 and one line on
  stderr, `netstead.<module> requires the [<extra>] extra: pip install 'netstead[<extra>]'`, which
  names the extra to install; `netstead doctor` shows which extras are present.

## Commands

{% raw %}
```text
Usage: netstead [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--install-completion` | flag |  | Install completion for the current shell. |
| `--show-completion` | flag |  | Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation. |

| Command | What it does | `--json` |
|---|---|---|
| [`netstead validate`](#netstead-validate) | Validate ``source`` against the GMNS spec. | yes |
| [`netstead info`](#netstead-info) | Print GMNS-aware metadata about ``source`` — spec version + table summary. | yes |
| [`netstead convert`](#netstead-convert) | Convert a data package from any supported format to another. | yes |
| [`netstead quality`](#netstead-quality) | Run the GMNS data-quality rule pack against ``source``. | yes |
| [`netstead doctor`](#netstead-doctor) | Check your netstead install — Python version, extras, vendored specs. | yes |
| [`netstead bench`](#netstead-bench) | Run read/validate/connectivity benchmarks; print timings. | yes |
| [`netstead bench-suite`](#netstead-bench-suite) | Run the DuckDB-path benchmark suite (create / selection / viz-pack). |  |
| [`netstead build`](#netstead-build) | Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture and write it to ``DEST``. | yes |
| [`netstead select`](#netstead-select) | Resolve a natural-language selection to GMNS link/node ids. | yes |
| [`netstead select-serve`](#netstead-select-serve) | Serve the interactive selection map: now an alias of ``netstead app SOURCE``. |  |
| [`netstead viz`](#netstead-viz) | Serve the network viewer: now an alias of ``netstead app SOURCE``. |  |
| [`netstead app`](#netstead-app) | Serve the Netstead Workbench: open, inspect, and select on GMNS networks in the browser. |  |
| [`netstead spec`](#netstead-spec) | GMNS spec utilities — list and diff vendored versions. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead server`](#netstead-server) | Run the netstead self-hostable HTTP server. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead mcp`](#netstead-mcp) | Run the netstead MCP server for AI-agent access. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead clean`](#netstead-clean) | GMNS network-editing ops (requires the 'clean' extra). | per sub-command |
| [`netstead scope`](#netstead-scope) | Build a NetworkScope and print its (links, nodes) sets. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead index`](#netstead-index) | Spatial + graph index build/status/drop. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead llm`](#netstead-llm) | Language-model providers for natural-language features. | per sub-command |

### `netstead validate`

Validate ``source`` against the GMNS spec.

Runs the four-pass validator (structural / schema / foreign-key
/ sync-state) with the GMNS spec auto-loaded — so reading a
CSV directory without a ``datapackage.json`` gets the real
per-table schema checks, not the empty "every table is
unexpected" output of the generic ``corral validate``.

Exit code is non-zero iff any ERROR-severity issue is recorded.

Examples:
    Validate the bundled Leavenworth fixture as CSVs::

```text
        $ netstead validate path/to/leavenworth/csv

    Write the interactive map+table HTML viewer::

        $ netstead validate path/to/network --html report.html

    Export findings to a spreadsheet::

        $ netstead validate path/to/network --csv f.csv --xlsx f.xlsx
```

```text
Usage: netstead validate [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path / URL to a GMNS network (datapackage.json or CSV/Parquet/DuckDB directory). |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--spec` | text |  | Override the default GMNS spec version (e.g. '0.96'). Defaults to netstead.DEFAULT_SPEC. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout instead of rich panels. |
| `--all` | flag |  | List every finding on its own row instead of folding repeated structural findings into one. |
| `--html` | path |  | Write the interactive network-on-map HTML viewer to this path. Falls back to a table-only HTML report when the \[reports\] extra is not installed. |
| `--csv` | path |  | Write the flat findings table to this CSV path. |
| `--xlsx` | path |  | Write the flat findings table to this XLSX path (requires \[reports\] extra). |
| `--yes`, `-y` | flag |  | Auto-approve any gated ops (alternative to CORRAL_AUTO_APPROVE=1). |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead info`

Print GMNS-aware metadata about ``source`` — spec version + table summary.

```text
Usage: netstead info [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path / URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--spec` | text |  | Override the default GMNS spec version. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout instead of rich panels. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead convert`

Convert a data package from any supported format to another.

Loads ``source`` (any format corral can read) and writes the
same logical package to ``dest`` in the target format. Output
format is taken from ``--format`` when supplied, otherwise
inferred from the ``dest`` extension; an extension-less ``dest``
defaults to partitioned parquet (architecture §6.1).

```text
Usage: netstead convert [OPTIONS] SOURCE DEST
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Source data package path/URL. |
| `DEST` | path | yes | Destination path. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--format`, `-f` | text |  | Output format (csv/parquet/duckdb/zipcsv). Default: infer from dest extension; fall back to parquet. |
| `--engine` | text |  | Engine: DuckDB (the only compute engine). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | flag |  | Auto-approve gated ops. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead quality`

Run the GMNS data-quality rule pack against ``source``.

Each rule emits Severity.WARNING / INFO findings with category
DATA_QUALITY. The output is a ValidationReport (rendered as a
rich table or JSON document per ``--json``).

```text
Usage: netstead quality [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path / URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--spec` | text |  | Override the default GMNS spec version. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout instead of rich panels. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead doctor`

Check your netstead install — Python version, extras, vendored specs.

```text
This is an INSTALL doctor, not a network doctor. To diagnose a
specific GMNS network, use:

  netstead validate <path>    spec / schema / FK / sync-state checks
  netstead quality  <path>    data-quality rules (high speed on residential, etc.)
  netstead info     <path>    table list + row counts
```

Exits non-zero on any install failure.

```text
Usage: netstead doctor [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit checks as a JSON array. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead bench`

Run read/validate/connectivity benchmarks; print timings.

Phases timed (each via time.perf_counter):

* ``load`` — `Network.from_source`.
* ``validate`` — `Network.validate` (structural/schema only).
* ``links_count`` + ``nodes_count`` — trivial materialization sanity.
* ``is_connected`` — full graph index build + component count
  (skipped silently when the ``[graph]`` extra is missing).

Output is a dict with ``phases`` (list of ``{phase, seconds}``) and
a ``total_seconds`` summary. ``--json`` writes the dict to stdout for
machine consumption; otherwise rendered via the standard rich panel.

```text
Usage: netstead bench [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path/URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead bench-suite`

Run the DuckDB-path benchmark suite (create / selection / viz-pack).

Sweeps the requested size tiers over the three operation families from
the benchmarking-suite scope, capturing wall-time and peak memory, and
emits one structured document. DuckDB (via ibis) is the single compute
engine; pandas / polars / pyarrow are I/O formats, so there is no engine
axis — the suite measures the DuckDB path and the binary store format.

``--format json`` (default) emits the canonical regression document;
``csv`` flattens the results; ``md`` renders the advertising table with
an environment stamp and the standing honesty caveats. Fixture
definitions live in ``benchmarks/fixtures.toml``; the L tier is resolved
from the ``NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE`` / ``NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE_BBOX`` env vars
(never committed).

```text
Usage: netstead bench-suite [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--sizes` | text | `S,M` | Size tiers to sweep (comma-separated: S,M,L). |
| `--operations` | text | `network_create,selection,viz_pack` | Operation families to run (comma-separated). |
| `--format` | text | `json` | Output format: json \| csv \| md. |
| `--output`, `-o` | path |  | Write to this file instead of stdout. |
| `--repeats` | integer | `3` | Macro timing repeats (reported as median + min). |
| `--warm-repeats` | integer | `20` | Repeats for the warm selection number. |
| `--run-osm` | flag |  | Include live OSM builds (hits Overpass). |
| `--fixtures` | path |  | Override path to a fixtures.toml. |
| `--commit` | text |  | Git SHA to stamp into the env block. |

### `netstead build`

Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture and write it to ``DEST``.

```text
Usage: netstead build [OPTIONS] DEST
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DEST` | path | yes | Output path for the GMNS network (dir or file). |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--place` | text |  | Place name to geocode (city/county/etc.). |
| `--bbox` | text |  | Bounding box 'west,south,east,north' (EPSG:4326). |
| `--point` | text |  | Center 'lat,lon'; use with --buffer. |
| `--buffer` | float | `0.0` | Buffer in metres around --point. |
| `--network-type` | text | `roads` | roads and/or paths; repeat the option or comma-separate (e.g. roads,paths). Deprecated: drive = roads; walk, bike, all = roads,paths. |
| `--extra-tags` | text |  | Comma-separated extra source properties/tags to carry. |
| `--source` | text | `osm` | Data source: 'osm' or 'overture'. |
| `--overture-release` | text |  | Overture release string (overture source only). |
| `--data-root` | text |  | Override Overture data base URI / local snapshot dir (overture source only). |
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--spec-version` | text |  | GMNS spec version (default: latest). |
| `--format` | text |  | Output format: csv / parquet / duckdb / zip. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit a JSON summary on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead select`

Resolve a natural-language selection to GMNS link/node ids.

Prints the validated selection fragment on success (exit 0). On an
ambiguous result it prints the status, the provisional link ids, each
anchor with the other nodes it could be, and diagnostics (exit 3); on
not-found it prints diagnostics (exit 1).

With a language model chosen and ``select.grammar_first`` on (the default),
the offline grammar is tried first and the model is called only when it
can't read the request with names the network has, as in the Workbench.

```text
Usage: netstead select [OPTIONS] UTTERANCE SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `UTTERANCE` | text | yes | e.g. "I-40 EB between Harrison Ave and NC 54". |
| `SOURCE` | text | yes | Path/URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--provider` | text |  | Parser: stub \| anthropic \| openai \| gemini \| ollama (default: settings). |
| `--model` | text |  | Model id (default: settings, else the provider default; see `netstead llm status`). |
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

| `--engine` | text |  | Ignored: DuckDB is the only engine (kept for compatibility). |
| `--host` | text |  | Bind host. |
| `--port` | integer |  | Bind port. |

### `netstead server`

Run the netstead self-hostable HTTP server.

```text
Usage: netstead server [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead server run`](#netstead-server-run) — Start the netstead HTTP server with config from ``--config``.

#### `netstead server run`

Start the netstead HTTP server with config from ``--config``.

Reads `corral.api.ServerSettings` from the config
file (or uses defaults — localhost, no packages, auth=bearer
with no token, which fails fast on first request).

The CLI ``--bind`` / ``--port`` flags override the matching
config keys for one-off testing without editing the file.

```text
Usage: netstead server run [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--config`, `-c` | path |  | Path to server config (YAML/JSON). |
| `--bind` | text |  | Override config bind address (default 127.0.0.1). |
| `--port` | integer |  | Override config port (default 8000). |


**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead mcp serve`](#netstead-mcp-serve) — Start the netstead MCP server on stdio (for Claude Desktop / Claude Code).

#### `netstead mcp serve`

Start the netstead MCP server on stdio (for Claude Desktop / Claude Code).

Configure your MCP client to launch ``netstead mcp serve`` as a
subprocess (typical example:

.. code-block:: json

```text
    {"mcpServers": {"netstead": {"command": "netstead", "args": ["mcp", "serve"]}}}
```

). Tools exposed: ``describe_network``, ``validate_package``,
``quality_check``, ``connected_components``, ``scope_from_nodes``,
plus the generic corral tools.

```text
Usage: netstead mcp serve [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--name` | text | `netstead` | MCP server display name. |


|---|---|---|---|
| `--yes`, `-y` | flag |  | Download without asking first. |

## Examples

Check the install, then summarize and validate a network. `--json` turns the summary into one
JSON document; `--html` writes the interactive validation report next to the terminal output.

```bash
netstead doctor
netstead info ./my-network --json
netstead validate ./my-network --html report.html
```

title: Schema reference
audience: both
kind: reference
summary: Field-level GMNS schema — every table and column of the official spec's master branch, rendered at build time (vendored 0.97 when offline).
---

# Official GMNS Specification

The GMNS specification is managed in the following Github repo: <https://github.com/zephyr-data-specs/GMNS>

This page renders the upstream `master` branch of that repository at docs build time: the macro fetches `Specification_md/datapackage.json` from GitHub and tabulates each resource and its schema. When the fetch fails (offline build, GitHub unreachable) it logs a warning and falls back to the vendored 0.97 spec at `packages/netstead/netstead/spec/0.97/`, so the tables below may be the vendored copy rather than the live branch.

| **GMNS Version** | **Description** |
| ----- | ----- |
| [development](../spec-versions/development.md) | Not yet in official spec. Hasn't been voted on by PMG |
| [local](../spec-versions/local.md) | Local copy of spec. May not be identical to official spec. |

GMNS is defined using the [Frictionless Framework](https://specs.frictionlessdata.io/#data-package-specs-suite) as a series of `tabular-data-resources`.

## Files in Specification

GMNS consists of a package of files as defined in the following table.

*The following tables are automatically generated from the official spec.*

{{ official_frictionless_spec('master') }}

## Data Table Schemas

{{ official_frictionless_schemas('master') }}

title: Table of tables
audience: both
kind: reference
summary: Catalog of every GMNS 0.97 resource — purpose, required vs optional, primary foreign keys, link into the field-level reference.
